Tischler and Piet Maes The citation for this ICTV Report chapter is the summary published as: Bradfute, S. B., Calisher, C. H., Klempa, B., Klingström, J., Kuhn, J. H., Laenen, L., Tischler, N. D., & Maes, P. (2024). ICTV Virus Taxonomy Profile: Hantaviridae 2024, Journal of General Virology 105, 001975 Corresponding author: Piet Maes ( [email protected] ) Edited by: Holly Hughes and Evelien Adriaenssens Posted: March 2024, updated June 2024 Summary Hantaviridae is a family for negative-sense RNA viruses with genomes of about 10.5–14.6 kb (Table 1 Hantaviridae ). The family includes eight genera ( Actinovirus and Percilovirus (subfamily Actantavirinae ), Agnathovirus (subfamily Agantavirinae ), Loanvirus , Mobatvirus , Orthohantavirus and Thottimvirus (subfamily Mammantavirinae ), and Reptillovirus (subfamily Repantavirinae ). These viruses are maintained in and/or transmitted by small mammals, but also by fish and reptiles. Several orthohantaviruses can infect humans, causing mild, severe, and sometimes-fatal diseases. Hantavirids produce enveloped virions containing three single-stranded RNA segments with open reading frames (ORFs) that encode a nucleoprotein (N), a glycoprotein precursor (GPC), and large (L) protein containing an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain. Table 1 Hantaviridae. Characteristics of members of the family Hantaviridae. Characteristic Description* Example Hantaan virus (S segment: M14626; M segment: M14627; L segment: X55901), species Orthohantavirus hantanense Virion Enveloped, pleomorphic virions 80–160 nm in diameter with heterodimeric surface spikes Genome Three single-stranded RNA molecules (segments): small (S; 1.0–3.0 kb), medium (M; 3.4–4.8 kb), and large (L; 5.3–6.8 kb) Replication Ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes containing anti-genomic RNA serve as coding templates for synthesis of genomic RNA Translation Proteins are produced from capped and non-polyadenylated mRNAs. The 5′-cap structure is obtained via cap-snatching from cellular mRNAs Host range Fish (actinoviruses, agnathoviruses, perciloviruses), mammals (orthohantaviruses), and reptiles (reptilloviruses) Taxonomy Realm Riboviria , kingdom Orthornavirae , phylum Negarnaviricota , class Bunyaviricetes , order Elliovirales ; the family includes four subfamilies, eight genera, and 55 species * mostly based on experiments with mammalian orthohantaviruses Viruses assigned to each of the seven genera form genus-specifc monophyletic clades based on phylogenetic analysis of concatenated L protein/RdRP, glycoprotein and N sequences. Viruses from all seven genera share one or more of the following characteristics: (i) enveloped pleomorphic virions; (ii) tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genome without polyadenylated tracts at the 3′-end; (iii) genomic sequence complementarity at the 5′- and 3′-ends; and (iv) capped but not polyadenylated virus mRNAs ( Maes et al., 2004 ). Piscine Hosts Genus Actinovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian (percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) fish. Genus Agnathovirus . Viruses in this genus infect agnathan (myxinid) fish. Genus Percilovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian ( gobiid, lophiid ) fish. Mammalian Hosts Genus Loanvirus. Viruses in this genus infect rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly nycterid bats and possibly murid rodents. Genus Mobatvirus. Viruses in this genus infect emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid and possibly molossid, and vespertillionid bats and soricid and talpid eulipotyphla. Genus Orthohantavirus. Viruses assigned to this genus infect soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Genus Thottimvirus. Viruses in this genus infect soricid and possibly talpid eulipotyphla. Reptilian Hosts Genus Reptillovirus . Viruses in this genus infect gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles. Virion Morphology Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Physicochemical and physical properties Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Nucleic acid Hantavirids have tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genomes (S, M, and L segments). The viral mRNAs are not polyadenylated and contain a 5′-methylated cap and several non-templated nucleotides at the 5′-end that are derived from host cell mRNAs via cap snatching ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Further information is only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Proteins Hantavirids typically express three structural proteins. The most abundant structural protein in a hantavirion is N, which encapsidates the hantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , are produced from GPC and mediate entry of hantavirions ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Spiropoulou 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Lipids Not reported but are likely derived from the Golgi apparatus and/or the host cell plasma membrane and therefore likely composed of phospholipids, glycolipids, fatty acids, and sterols. Carbohydrates Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Genome organization and replication S RNA encodes N and in some viruses NSs ( Jääskeläinen et al., 2007 , Vera-Otarola et al., 2012 ), M RNA encodes GPC, and the L RNA encodes L with its RdRP, helicase, and endonuclease domains ( Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 ) (Figure 1 Hantaviridae ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Figure 1 Hantaviridae . Genome organization of representative hantaviruses. The 5′- and 3′- ends of all segments are complementary at their termini, likely promoting the formation of panhandle RNP complexes within the virion . GPC , glycoprotein precursor gene; L , large (protein) gene; N , nucleoprotein gene. Biology Hantavirids have been found in actinopterygian (gobiid, lophiid, percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) and agnathan (myxinid) fish; in emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid, rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly molossid and nycterid bats; in soricid and talpid eulipotyphla; in muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents; in gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles; and potentially in coleopteran and plectopteran insects (see genus pages for details). Only orthohantaviruses are known to cause diseases (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Antigenicity Systematic antigenicity studies have only been reported for orthohantaviruses (see Orthohantavirus genus page). species demarcation criteria The availability of at least coding-complete sequences of all three genome segments may be sufficient for hantavirid classification in the absence of a cultured isolate. Demarcation of genera is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Hantaviridae: current classification and future perspectives, Viruses, 11, 9, e0788">Laenen et al., 2019 ). DEmARC analysis gave a frequency distribution of Pairwise Evolutionary Distance (PED) values of which the threshold of 0.1 gave an optimal clustering cost of zero and is used as the hantavirid species demarcation criterium. Genera are demarked by a PED-value threshold of 0.95 and subfamilies are demarcated based on their distinct clustering in a Bayesian maximum clade credibility tree and a PED-value threshold of 3.5. Relationships within the family Phylogenetic relationships across the family have been estimated using Bayesian maximum clade credibility trees generated from complete N, GPC, and L amino-acid sequences; similar topologies are obtained with concatenated N and GPC sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Figure 2 Hantaviridae . Maximum likelihood phylogenetic tree inferred using IQ-TREE. The tree was constructed based on 53 concatenated S and M segment (amino acid) sequences using the LG+R9 model of sequence evolution. Branch lengths represent the estimated number of substitutions per site. Bootstrap support values (>70%) are indicated at nodes, reflecting the degree of confidence in the branching pattern. Relationships with other taxa Hantavirids are closely related to bunyaviral crulivirids, fimovirids, peribunyavirids, phasmavirids, tulasvirids, and tospovirids ( Wolf et al., 2018 , Herath et al., 2020 ). Using the Master Species List Using the Virus Metadata Resource Using the Find the Species tool Using the ICTV Report Webinar Webinar on Virus Taxonomy Webinar on Finding Information GitHub Repository Zenodo Repository Email ICTV Help ‏‏‎ ‎ ICTV Report Book: Hantaviridae Family: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Actantavirinae Genus: Actinovirus Genus: Percilovirus Subfamily: Agantavirinae Genus: Agnathovirus Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Loanvirus Genus: Mobatvirus Genus: Orthohantavirus Genus: Thottimvirus Subfamily: Repantavirinae Genus: Reptillovirus Authors: Hantaviridae Citation: Hantaviridae References: Hantaviridae Resources: Hantaviridae Species List: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Orthohantavirus Distinguishing features Sixty different viruses are classified in the genus Orthohantavius. These viruses typically infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease in humans ( Schmaljohn and Hjelle 1997 , Jonsson et al., 2010 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 , Vial et al., 2023 ). Virion Morphology Orthohantavirions are pleomorphic in shape, mostly spherical of 80–160 nm in diameter ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ), and surrounded by a membrane envelope that is decorated with glycoprotein (GP) spikes composed of G N and G C subunits (Figure 1 Orthohantavirus ). The virion envelope is 5 nm thick and is decorated with square shaped spikes, consisting of tetrameric G N -G C heterodimers, which protrude 10 nM from the membrane forming a surface lattice of local symmetry interrupted by empty membrane spots ( Hung et al., 1983 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Parvate et al., 2019 , Serris et al., 2020 , Guardado-Calvo and Rey 2021 ). Isolated ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes are composed of individual segment genomic RNA encapsidated by nucleoprotein (N) ( Tao et al., 1987 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Hepojoki et al., 2012 , Guo et al., 2016 , Arragain et al., 2019 ). Virions assemble and bud from the Golgi complex or cell surface membranes, depending on the virus ( Goldsmith et al., 1995 , Parvate et al., 2019 ). Figure 1 Orthohantavirus. A, B) Electron micrographs of Tula virus particles adapted from ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ). C) Schematic illustration of an orthohantavirus particle. Shown is a spherical and enveloped (grey) particle with glycoprotein spikes (G N yellow, G C blue) inserted in a bilaminar lipid envelope. The S (small), M (medium), and L (large) RNP (ribonucleoprotein) complexes inside the particle consist of N (nucleoprotein, green) and L (large protein, pink). ViralZone image reproduced courtesy of SwissBioPics. Physicochemical and physical properties Virion buoyant densities in sucrose and CsCl are 1.15–1.18 ( White et al., 1982 ) and 1.20–1.21 g cm −3 , respectively ( Schmaljohn et al., 1983 ). Virions are sensitive to chemical inactivation with, for instance, methanol, paraformaldehyde, acetone/methanol, N -ethylmaleimide or detergents, as well as physical methods such as heat, gamma irradiation or UV irradiation ( Kraus et al., 2005 , Strandin et al., 2011 , Elveborg et al., 2022 ). Nucleic acid Orthohantavirus genomes are linear tri-segmented RNA molecules of negative polarity. The genomes are about 11.1–12.3 kb in length (small [S] segment: 1.2–2.1 kb; medium [M] segment: 3.4–3.8 kb; large [L] segment: 6.5–6.6 kb). Proteins Orthohantaviruses typically express three structural proteins (Table 1 Orthohantavirus ). The most abundant structural protein in an orthohantavirion is N, which encapsidates the orthohantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , mediate virion entry. G N and G C and non-structural proteins are encoded as a precursor polyprotein. Table 1 Orthohantavirus . Location and function of orthohantavirus structural proteins. Protein Location, mass, and function Reference Nucleoprotein (N) Structural virion protein (about 48 kD). Oligomerizes and encapsidates orthohantaviral genomic segments and hence component of RNPs. Binds to L and G N ( Mir et al., 2010 , Reuter and Krüger 2018 , Arragain et al., 2019 ) Nonstructural protein (NSs) Non-structural protein encoded by some orhtohantaviruses. Has type I interferon inhibitory activity. May occur as multiple isoforms. ( Vera-Otarola et al., 2020 , Binder et al., 2021 ) Glycoprotein (GP) Structural virion protein consisting of two subunits (G N : about 70-75 kD, G C : about 50-55 kD). Produced via proteolytic cleavage from the genome-encoded precursor GPC. Projects from virion membranes as tetrameric GP spikes composed of G N and G C heterodimers. GP mediates cell- receptor binding; as a class II fusion machine it induces virion-cell membrane fusion and, thereby cell entry. G N binds to N and RNA ( Spiropoulou et al., 2003 , Tischler et al., 2005 , Cifuentes-Muñoz et al., 2014 , Li et al., 2016 , Willensky et al., 2016 , Rissanen et al., 2017 , Zhu et al., 2018 , Bignon et al., 2019 , Sperber et al., 2019 ) Large protein (L) Structural virion protein (246 kD) with RdRP, helicase, and endoribonuclease domains. Component of the RNP inside virions. Binds to N and RNA. Oligomerizes and mediates transcription and replication of viral RNA segments. Mediates cap-snatching for viral mRNA capping. ( Kukkonen et al., 2005 , Cheng et al., 2014 , Rothenberger et al., 2016 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Durieux Trouilleton et al., 2023 ) Genome organization and replication The orthohantavirus genome consists of three negative-sense RNA molecules, termed S (small), M (medium), and L (large) (Figure 2 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 2 Orthohantavirus. Schematic representation of orthohantavirus genome organization. Orthohantavirus genomic segments assume circular forms via non-covalent binding of complementary and highly conserved 3′- and 5′-terminal sequences. Genomic segment reassortment mostly occurs among viruses belonging to the same species but interspecies reassortment likely occurs occasionally ( Klempa 2018 , Petazzi et al., 2021 ). Orthohantavirus infection starts with virion attachment, mediated by G N and G C , to cell-surface attachment factors and entry via the endosomal route ( Shtanko et al., 2014 ) (Figure 3 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 3 Orthohantavirus . Lifecycle of orthohantaviruses. (1) Virion attachment; (2) virion uptake; (3) virion-cell membrane fusion; (4) transcription; (5) translation; (6) replication; (7) virion assembly; and (8) virion egress. After engaging a cellular receptor, protocadherin 1 in the case of American orthohantaviruses, virion-membrane fusion results in early or late endosomal release, depending on the virus, of the virion RNP complex into the cytoplasm in a pH-dependent manner ( Jangra et al., 2018 , Mittler et al., 2019 , Torriani et al., 2019 , Dieterle et al., 2021 ). During primary transcription L generates uncapped antigenomic RNA molecules that are then capped using host cell-derived capped primers (cap snatching). L and S segment-transcribed mRNAs are translated by free ribosomes ( Garcin et al., 1995 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Meier et al., 2021 ). M segment-transcribed mRNA is translated by membrane-bound ribosomes, with the expressed GPC which is likely co-translationally cleaved by cellular proteases to yield G N and G C . The synthesis of the antigenome by L protein serves as a template for genomic RNA replication. Secondary transcription amplifies the synthesis of mRNAs and genome replication. During morphogenesis, G N and G C accumulate in the Golgi apparatus, modified host membranes are acquired, and virions bud into the Golgi. Biology Genus Orthohantavirus includes 38 species for 60 distinct viruses. These viruses and their unclassified, potential relatives, subclinically, and often chronically, infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla, and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents ( Jonsson et al., 2010 , Wu et al., 2018 , Chen et al., 2023 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are overall distributed worldwide, but the individual geographic distribution is dependent on host range. At least some orthohantaviruses may not be as restricted to a particular host as originally thought, but may be carried by animals of multiple hosts ( Goodfellow et al., 2021 , Quizon et al., 2022 , Gu et al., 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease (all in humans) and all disease-causing viruses are rodent-borne. Human infection may occur after inhalation of aerosolized excreta or secreta of infected rodents or direct rodent contact. The two WHO-recognized orthohantavirus-caused diseases are hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), caused by Asian and European viruses (in particular Dobrava virus [DOBV], Hantaan virus [HTNV], Puumala virus [PUUV] and Seoul virus [SEOV]), and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a frequently lethal disease caused by viruses from the Americas (in particular Andes virus [ANDV] and Sin Nombre virus [SNV]) ( Vial et al., 2023 ). The hamster model of wild-type ANDV infection is lethal and largely mimics human HPS ( Hooper et al., 2001 ). After SNV infection in nonhuman primates, some animals develop an HPS-like disease, but cell passage of SNV can result in mutations that render the virus non-pathogenic in this model ( Safronetz et al., 2014 ). Many rodent models result in a chronic, asymptomatic infection, and these have been used in early-stage therapeutic studies ( Strandin et al., 2020 ). However, recent advances have been made in development of an HFRS mouse model using HTNV variants ( Wei et al., 2022 ). Orthohantavirus animal models are reviewed in ( Golden et al., 2015 ). Antigenicity There is considerable serum cross-reactivity between the nucleocapsids of hantavirids, but neutralizing antibodies targeting Gn/Gc are more specific. SNV was first identified as a hantavirid based on cross-reactivity of patient sera with other orthohantavirus antigens ( 1993 ). Similarly, rodents that carried SNV were identified in serosurveys using non-SNV orthohantavirus antigens, since SNV had not been isolated at the time ( Childs et al., 1994 ). Species demarcation criteria Demarcation of species is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Laenen et al., 2019 ). Phylogenetic relationships across the genus have been estimated using maximum likelihood trees generated from complete N, GPC and L amino-acid sequences, and for N and GPC amino-acid sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Hantaviridae ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Hantaviridae (taxid:1980413) VIRION Enveloped, spherical. Diameter from 80 to 120nm. GENOME Segmented Negative-stranded RNA linear genome, L segment is between 6.8 and 12 kb, M segment between 3.2 and 4.9 kb and S segment between 1 and 3 kb. Encodes for four to six proteins. Some hantaviruses also encode a NSs protein on their S segment. GENE EXPRESSION The viral RNA dependent RNA polymerase (L) binds to a promoter on each encapsidated segment, and transcribes the mRNA. These are capped by L protein during synthesis using cap snatching . Transcription is terminated by a strong hairpin sequence at the end of each gene. Puumala virus expressed an additional NSs by leaky scanning in the NS gene. ENZYMES RNA-dependent RNA polymerase L Cap Snatching endonuclease L REPLICATION CYTOPLASMIC Virus attaches to host receptors though Gn-Gc glycoprotein dimer, and is endocytosed into vesicles in the host cell. Fusion of virus membrane with the vesicle membrane; ribonucleocapsid segments are released in the cytoplasm. Transcription , viral mRNAs are capped in the cytoplasm. Replication presumably starts when enough nucleoprotein is present to encapsidate neo-synthetized antigenomes and genomes. The ribonucleocapsids buds at Golgi apparatus, releasing the virion by exocytosis. The hantaviruses (Hantaviridae) ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Back to Andes virus resource There are approximately 92 known viruses in the family Hantaviridae, classified into 52 species. Each species is typically adapted to a specific reservoir host, most commonly rodents, but also bats and moles. With the notable exception of Andes virus, hantaviruses are generally not transmitted from person to person. Based on their geographic distribution, evolutionary relationships, and the diseases they cause in humans, hantaviruses can be broadly divided into three major groups: New World hantaviruses (the Americas) These viruses cause Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a severe respiratory disease. Important examples include Sin Nombre virus and Andes virus. Annual incidence are about 100 cases per year (Andes virus) about 25 cases per year (Sin Nombre virus) Old World hantaviruses (Asia) These viruses are responsible for Hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), which is characterized by fever, hemorrhage, and acute kidney injury. Major examples include Hantaan virus and Seoul virus. Annual incidence: more than 10,000 cases worldwide Old World hantaviruses (Europe) European hantaviruses typically cause a milder form of HFRS known as Nephropathia epidemica (NE). The main causative agents are Puumala virus and Dobrava-Belgrade virus. Annual incidence: more than 1,000 cases Together, these viruses represent an important and diverse group of zoonotic pathogens that can cause severe disease following accidental transmission from their natural animal hosts to humans.

papers.title: Epidemiology and economic burden of Puumala virus infection in Styria, Austria, 2003 to 2024
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Hantavirus infections cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and impose a potential burden on healthcare systems. However, comprehensive economic data remain scarce. We quantified the inpatient economic burden of hospitalized patients with Puumala virus (PUUV) infections in Styria, Austria ́s primary endemic region, to identify hospitalization costs and early admission predictors of costs. Methods This retrospective cost-of-illness study analyzed 1,049 serologically confirmed PUUV hospitalizations across 20 public hospitals in Styria, Austria between September 2003 and March 2024. Costs were estimated using the Austrian performance-oriented hospital financing (LKF) diagnosis-related-group-system, standardized to 2024-equivalent Euros using consumer-price-index deflation. Admission predictors of cost were assessed using multivariable γ-generalized-linear-modeling with multiple imputation. Temporal trends in length of stay were analyzed using weighted segmented linear regression. Results Cumulative inpatient cost was approximately €10.3 million (mean per-case: €9,788) for the entire study period of 21 years. Three epidemic years (2012, 2019, 2021) accounted for 53.6% of cases and over €5.2 million in expenditure, with peak annual costs reaching €1.93 million (0.274% of total Styrian inpatient expenditure) in 2012. Prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT; cost-ratio 1.024 per second, 95% CI 1.019–1.030) and older age (CR 1.004 per year, 95%-CI 1.001–1.008) were independent admission-level predictors of higher cost. Median hospital length of stay declined by approximately 50% over the study period. Conclusions PUUV hospitalizations impose a sharply episodic but recurrent economic burden on regional healthcare systems. Admission aPTT and age independently predicted cost, but clinical outcomes were not modelled and these variables do not constitute a triage tool. Epidemic preparedness strategies are warranted.

source_records.title: Epidemiology and economic burden of Puumala virus infection in Styria, Austria, 2003 to 2024
source_records.abstract: Abstract Background Hantavirus infections cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and impose a potential burden on healthcare systems. However, comprehensive economic data remain scarce. We quantified the inpatient economic burden of hospitalized patients with Puumala virus (PUUV) infections in Styria, Austria ́s primary endemic region, to identify hospitalization costs and early admission predictors of costs. Methods This retrospective cost-of-illness study analyzed 1,049 serologically confirmed PUUV hospitalizations across 20 public hospitals in Styria, Austria between September 2003 and March 2024. Costs were estimated using the Austrian performance-oriented hospital financing (LKF) diagnosis-related-group-system, standardized to 2024-equivalent Euros using consumer-price-index deflation. Admission predictors of cost were assessed using multivariable γ-generalized-linear-modeling with multiple imputation. Temporal trends in length of stay were analyzed using weighted segmented linear regression. Results Cumulative inpatient cost was approximately €10.3 million (mean per-case: €9,788) for the entire study period of 21 years. papers.full_text: Abstract Background Andes orthohantavirus (ANDV) is a rodent-borne, tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA virus that causes hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome in southern South America. Most infections follow exposure to dust, surfaces, or particles contaminated with urine, faeces, or saliva from infected reservoir rodents. ANDV is unusual among hantaviruses because limited person-to-person transmission has been reported in Argentina and Chile. Main body This critical narrative review evaluates ANDV taxonomy, genetic diversity, reservoir ecology, patient shedding, outbreak epidemiology, transmission mechanisms, and countermeasures from a One Health perspective. The evidence supports a narrow conclusion: ANDV can spread between people, especially after close, prolonged, household, caregiving, nosocomial, or intimate exposure. Recent studies showing viral RNA, and sometimes infectious virus, in blood, oral, nasopharyngeal, urine, and other compartments strengthen the biological plausibility of close-contact transmission. However, RNA detection, body-fluid infectivity, similar viral genomes, and co-housing animal transmission do not by themselves show routine casual airborne spread. Most disease still follows rodent-associated environmental exposure, and shared environmental exposure remains a major confounder in endemic areas. Short conclusion ANDV should not be described as non-transmissible between humans, but it should also not be framed as an efficient airborne respiratory virus. Preparedness should combine rodent-exposure reduction, early clinical recognition, isolation and body-fluid precautions for suspected cases, contact monitoring, paired human-rodent sequencing, updated serosurveys, and continued development of vaccines, antibody-based therapies, and early antivirals. analysis.main_directions: The review critically evaluates ANDV taxonomy, genetic diversity, reservoir ecology, patient shedding, outbreak epidemiology, transmission mechanisms, and countermeasures from a One Health perspective (F4).
analysis.current_state: Evidence supports that ANDV can spread between people after close, prolonged household, caregiving, nosocomial, or intimate exposure, but it is not an efficient airborne respiratory virus; rodent‑associated environmental exposure remains the dominant source (F5, F9).

analysis.summary_en: Background: Andes orthohantavirus causes HCPS in southern South America and has limited person‑to‑person spread, prompting a One Health review. Main directions: The review covers taxonomy, genetics, reservoir ecology, shedding, epidemiology, transmission mechanisms, and countermeasures. Current state: ANDV can transmit between humans after close, prolonged contact but is not an efficient airborne virus; rodent exposure remains primary. Gaps: The role of casual airborne spread, infectivity of body‑fluid RNA, and environmental confounding are unresolved. Future research: Integrated surveillance with rodent control, early detection, isolation, body‑fluid precautions, paired sequencing, serosurveys, and development of vaccines, antibody therapies, and antivirals is needed.

papers.title_zh: 安第斯病毒 与人际传播:一项关键的 One Health 综述

analysis_zh.background: 安第斯病毒 正汉坦病毒 (ANDV) 在南美洲南部导致 汉坦病毒心肺综合征,并已报告有限的人际传播,促使进行 One Health 综述 (F1, F3)。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 本综述从 One Health 视角对 ANDV 的分类学、遗传多样性、宿主生态、患者病毒排泄、疫情流行病学、传播机制以及对策进行批判性评估 (F4)。
analysis_zh.current_state: 证据表明,ANDV 可在密切、长期的家庭、护理、院内或亲密接触后在人与人之间传播,但其并非高效的空气呼吸道病毒;啮齿动物相关的环境暴露仍是主要来源 (F5, F9)。
analysis_zh.gaps: 关于偶发空气传播、不同体液中检测到的 RNA 的感染性,以及共享环境暴露对人际传播评估的混淆程度仍存在不确定性 (F7, F8)。
analysis_zh.future_research: 防备工作应结合降低啮齿动物暴露、早期临床识别、隔离与体液防护、接触者监测、人鼠配对测序、更新的血清流行病学调查,以及持续研发疫苗、抗体疗法和早期抗病毒药物 (F10)。

papers.summary_zh: 背景:安第斯病毒 正汉坦病毒 (ANDV) 在南美洲南部导致 汉坦病毒心肺综合征,并已报告有限的人际... 主要方向:本综述从 One Health 视角对 ANDV 的分类学、遗传多样性、宿主生态、患者病毒排泄... 研究现状:证据表明,ANDV 可在密切、长期的家庭、护理、院内或亲密接触后在人与人之间传播,但其并非高效... 不足:关于偶发空气传播、不同体液中检测到的 RNA 的感染性,以及共享环境暴露对人际传播评估的混淆程... 后续研究:防备工作应结合降低啮齿动物暴露、早期临床识别、隔离与体液防护、接触者监测、人鼠配对测序、更新的...

papers.title: Hantavirus infections: A growing global health concern.
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses are increasingly regarded as an important emerging risk to global health, with an estimated annual impact on more than 200000 people worldwide. These pathogens are single-stranded RNA viruses belonging to the family Han taviridae and are known to cause two major clinical syndromes in humans: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS). The so-called old world hantaviruses, which are associated with HFRS, are predominantly distributed across Asia, Europe, and parts of Africa. In contrast, new world hantaviruses, responsible for HPS, are largely confined to North and South America. Each year, approximately 150000-200000 HFRS cases require hospitalization globally, with the greatest burden occurring in developing regions. The mortality rate of HFRS ranges from below 1% to about 12%, depending on the infecting strain. Both disease forms are characterized by increased capillary permeability, leading to clinical features such as hypotension, thrombocytopenia, and leukocytosis. While HFRS has a broader geographic distribution, HPS carries a higher risk of death. Moreover, the detection of new viral strains and the steady rise in reported cases have intensified global concern. Enhancing surveillance systems and expanding laboratory diagnostic capacity are therefore essential for effective monitoring and control of hantavirus diseases.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are increasingly regarded as an emerging global health risk affecting more than 200,000 people annually.
analysis.main_directions: The review outlines the virology of single‑stranded RNA hantaviruses, the two principal clinical syndromes (HFRS and HPS), and their geographic distribution.
analysis.current_state: Old‑world hantaviruses cause HFRS mainly in Asia, Europe and Africa, while New‑world hantaviruses cause HPS in the Americas; HFRS accounts for 150‑200 k hospitalizations yearly with mortality ranging from <1% to ~12% depending on strain.
analysis.gaps: Detection of novel strains and a steady rise in reported cases reveal surveillance gaps, and limited laboratory diagnostic capacity hampers timely case identification.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses are increasingly regarded as an emerging global health risk affecting >200,000 people annually. Main directions: The review outlines the virology of single‑stranded RNA hantaviruses, the two principal clinical syndromes (HFRS and HPS), and their geographic distribution. Current state: Old‑world hantaviruses cause HFRS in Asia, Europe and Africa, New‑world hantaviruses cause HPS in the Americas; HFRS causes 150‑200 k hospitalizations yearly with mortality <1%–12% by strain. Gaps: Novel strain detection and rising case numbers expose surveillance gaps and limited diagnostic capacity. Future research: Strengthen global surveillance and expand laboratory diagnostics to better monitor and control hantavirus disease.

papers.title_zh: 汉坦病毒感染:日益突出的全球健康问题。

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒es 正在日益被视为一种新兴的全球健康风险,每年影响超过200,000人。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 本综述概述了单链RNA 汉坦病毒es 的病毒学、两种主要临床综合征(HFRS(肾综合征出血热)和 HPS(汉坦病毒肺综合征))以及其地理分布。
analysis_zh.current_state: 旧世界 汉坦病毒es 主要在亚洲、欧洲和非洲导致 HFRS(肾综合征出血热),而新世界 汉坦病毒es 在美洲导致 HPS(汉坦病毒肺综合征);HFRS 每年导致 150‐200 千例住院,死亡率因株而异,范围为 <1% 至约 12%。
analysis_zh.gaps: 新毒株的检测以及报告病例的持续上升揭示了监测空白,实验室诊断能力有限阻碍了病例的及时识别。
analysis_zh.future_research: 建议加强全球监测网络并扩大诊断实验室能力,以提升对 汉坦病毒 疾病的监测和控制。

papers.summary_zh: 背景：汉坦病毒es 正在日益被视为一种新兴的全球健康风险,每年影响超过200,000人。 主要方向：本综述概述了单链RNA 汉坦病毒es 的病毒学、两种主要临床综合征(HFRS(肾综合征出血热)和 HPS(汉坦病毒肺综合征))以及其地理分布。 研究现状：旧世界 汉坦病毒es 主要在亚洲、欧洲和非洲导致 HFRS(肾综合征出血热),而新世界 汉坦病毒es 在美洲导致 HPS(汉坦病毒肺综合征);… 不足：新毒株的检测以及报告病例的持续上升揭示了监测空白,实验室诊断能力有限阻碍了病例的及时识别。 后续研究：建议加强全球监测网络并扩大诊断实验室能力,以提升对 汉坦病毒 疾病的监测和控制。

papers.title: Hantavirus: A Dangerous Scientific Cruise
papers.abstract: Thirteen cases of hantavirus infection (including three deaths) were detected on a cruise ship returning from Ushuaia. Following discussions, the ship was permitted to dock in the Canary Islands, where passengers were disembarked under safety protocols and sent back to their respective countries for medical monitoring. Hantaviruses comprise more than 53 species, each associated with a specific rodent. Humans become infected through the inhalation of excreta in areas frequented by rodents. Hantavirus infections are zoonoses that manifest as hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome or cardiopulmonary syndrome. The Andes strain, found in South America, is capable of human-to-human transmission. Diagnosis is established via serology or PCR. There is no treatment or vaccine.
papers.journal: International Journal of Medical Parasitology and Epidemiology Sciences

papers.full_text: Introduction Every year, many people travel on cruise ships. In 2025, 87 million travelers enjoyed cruises, according to the cruise industry. It is therefore not surprising that infections such as gastroenteritis can spread quickly within the confined space of a boat. However, other, rarer infections can also occur. A few months ago, the Dutch-flagged cruise ship MV Hondrius (Figure 1) departed from the port of Ushuaia bound for Cape Verde. However, a stowaway disrupted the voyage: the hantavirus. This incident immediately brought to mind events from a few years ago involving the Diamond Princess, a cruise ship stranded in Japan during the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic. Yet, in this instance, the virus is different, and the risk of transmission appears to be extremely low. Infection prior to boarding This ship was not intended for a typical tourist cruise but carried 150 people of 23 nationalities, primarily ornithologists, botanists, cetacean specialists, and history and geography enthusiasts. After Ushuaia, the ship stopped at St. Helena Island, where about thirty passengers disembarked and flew home. So, two options regarding the management of patients on board the ship quickly circulated. analysis.background: Thirteen cases of hantavirus infection, including three deaths, were detected on a cruise ship returning from Ushuaia (A1). Hantavirus infections are zoonoses that can cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome or cardiopulmonary syndrome, posing a public‑health threat (A5).
analysis.methods: The ship carried about 150 passengers of 23 nationalities (F9) and, after discussions, was allowed to dock in the Canary Islands where passengers were disembarked under safety protocols (A2). WHO teams collected over 150 rodent samples, all testing negative (F16). Diagnosis of the cases was performed by serology or PCR (A7).
analysis.results: A total of 13 laboratory‑confirmed cases were identified, with three fatalities, giving a mortality of 27.3% (A1; A36). Eight patients showed symptoms and three died (F13). One patient required intensive care while 25 contact persons remained negative (F32).
analysis.contribution: The report documents a hantavirus outbreak on a cruise ship, highlighting the zoonotic risk of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome or cardiopulmonary syndrome in confined travel settings (A5). It notes that the Andes strain can transmit between humans (A6) and that no specific treatment or vaccine exists (A8), underscoring the need for surveillance and infection‑control measures.
analysis.limitations: The evidence is limited to a single descriptive case series with a small number of cases (A1) and rodent sampling was restricted to one location with all negatives (F16). No controlled epidemiologic study, viral sequencing, or treatment evaluation was reported.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Thirteen hantavirus cases (three deaths) occurred on a cruise ship, illustrating a serious zoonotic threat (A1, A5). Methods: About 150 passengers were examined; the ship docked under safety protocols, WHO collected >150 rodent samples (all negative), and diagnoses used serology or PCR (A2, F9, F16, A7). Results: Thirteen confirmed cases with 27.3% mortality, eight symptomatic patients, three deaths, one ICU case, and 25 contacts negative (A1, A36, F13, F32). Contribution: The case highlights hantavirus risk on cruises, the potential for human‑to‑human transmission of the Andes strain, and the lack of treatment or vaccine (A5, A6, A8). Limitations: Findings derive from a single small outbreak report with limited rodent sampling and no controlled study or viral sequencing (A1, F16).

analysis_zh.background: 在从乌斯怀亚返航的邮轮上检测到13例 汉坦病毒 感染病例,其中包括3例死亡 (A1)。汉坦病毒 感染属于人畜共患病,可导致 肾综合征出血热 或心肺综合征,构成公共卫生威胁 (A5)。
analysis_zh.methods: 该船载有约150名来自23个国家的乘客 (F9),经协商后获准在加那利群岛停靠,乘客在安全协议下下船 (A2)。世卫组织团队采集了150余只啮齿动物样本,全部检测为阴性 (F16)。病例诊断采用血清学或PCR方法 (A7)。
analysis_zh.results: 共确认实验室检测阳性的13例病例,其中3例死亡,死亡率为27.3% (A1; A36)。8名患者出现症状,3例死亡 (F13)。1名患者需接受重症监护,25名密切接触者检测为阴性 (F32)。
analysis_zh.contribution: 本报告记录了邮轮上发生的 汉坦病毒 爆发,强调在封闭旅行环境中 肾综合征出血热 或心肺综合征的人畜共患风险 (A5)。报告指出安第斯病毒株可在人际间传播 (A6),且目前缺乏特异性治疗或疫苗 (A8),强调需加强监测和感染控制措施。
analysis_zh.limitations: 证据仅限于单一描述性病例系列,病例数较少 (A1),且啮齿动物采样仅在一处进行,全部为阴性 (F16)。未报告受控流行病学研究、病毒测序或治疗评估。

papers.title: Hantavirus QSP Model: Ribavirin, Favipiravir, and Combination Antiviral Therapy
papers.abstract: Every figure, table and quoted value in the associated manuscript is generated by code in this release and checked back against the text. New analyses: mechanism_weights.R decomposes the placebo trajectory so the share each module contributes to the reported outcome is derived rather than asserted; rebound_diagnostics.R separates the on-treatment plateau from the post-withdrawal rebound; identifiability_profile.R keeps the parameter values the calibration datum cannot reject; identifiability_joint.R applies the same criterion with all 32 parameters varying together; reference_numbers.R looks citation numbers up in the bibliography so renumbering cannot silently invalidate a figure; reproduce_manuscript.R runs every analysis in dependency order. Checks: check_numbers.py re-derives every value quoted in the results and fails on a mismatch, check_package.py checks citations, captions, footnotes and figure resolution, and check_provenance.py maps each display item to the script that writes it. Corrections those checks found: the combination ablation was reported against the wrong scenario, the on-treatment infected-cell count and two mortality values were misrounded, a clearance correlation was wrong at two decimals, and a quasi-steady-state bound held only at one solver step size. All 122 tests pass and the pipeline reproduces bit for bit. The Zenodo concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20558774 is version-agnostic and resolves to this release.

papers.title: Clinical severity and health-seeking behaviors of cases with hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome: A comparative study across spatial clusters in Jiangxi Province, China
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a significant public health concern in Jiangxi Province, China, where both Hantaan (HTNV) and Seoul (SEOV) co-circulate. Previous studies have identified three distinct clusters of HFRS epidemic in Jiangxi Province, characterized by geographical separation and heterogeneous incidence levels. We hypothesized that clinical severity and healthcare-seeking behaviors may vary across these clusters, and thus conducted a retrospective study to examine this hypothesis. METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 4,614 HFRS cases (13-year period) from 63 counties. Cases were classified into four areas based on prior spatial study, representing distinct hilly and plain regions with different proximity to major water bodies and mountains. Data on HFRS cases were collected by county-level CDC staff using a nationally standardized case investigation questionnaire. Clinical severity and healthcare-seeking behaviors (hospital level, onset-to-visit interval) were compared. RESULTS: HFRS cases in Cluster I exhibited the highest clinical severity (22.41% severe, 6.65% critical), while cases in Cluster II were strikingly mild (2.62% severe, 1.31% critical). Median onset-to-visit interval was longest in Cluster II (5 days) vs others (2-4 days). Hospital preference varied: Cluster I primarily used Class II hospitals (65.88%); Cluster II showed near-equal use of Class II (48.44%) and III (47.01%); Cluster III and non-clustered areas favored higher-level hospitals. CONCLUSION: Our findings confirmed that Jiangxi Province, though a mixed epidemic focus, exhibited distinct spatial heterogeneity in clinical severity, and healthcare-seeking behaviors. These findings underscore the need for regionally tailored strategies in HFRS prevention and control.

Author summary Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a serious infectious disease in China, with thousands of cases reported annually. Previous studies have shown that cases in Jiangxi Province tend to cluster in specific geographic areas. How­ ever, it remained unclear whether patients in these different areas experienced different disease outcomes or sought care in different ways. In this study, we analyzed data from more than 4,600 patients across 63 counties over 13 years. We found that disease severity and how quickly people sought care differed sub­ stantially between regions. Patients in Cluster I were much more likely to devel­ op severe or critical illness, whereas cases in Cluster II were predominantly mild. We also identified significant inter-regional differences in healthcare-seeking behavior, including time to initial care and choice of healthcare facility. Cluster I patients predominantly utilized Class II hospitals, while those in other regions more often presented directly to Class III hospitals. These findings show that HFRS affects different parts of Jiangxi Province in different ways. This means that public health strategies—such as health education campaigns and hospital resource planning—should be tailored to the specific needs of each region, rath­ er than using a one-size-fits-all approach. Introduction Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a rodent-borne zoonotic disease caused by hantavirus (HVs) infection [1,2]. Humans are mainly infected through being bitten by infected host animals, inhaling or directly contacting their excre­ tions and contaminants [3]. The etiology of HFRS exhibits geographic variation: it is primarily caused by Hantaan (HTNV) and Seoul (SEOV) viruses in Asia, and by Puumala (PUUV) and Dobrava-Belgrade (DOBV) viruses in Europe, where the infec­ tion often presents as the milder nephropathia epidemica (NE) [4]. China bears the highest global burden of HFRS, accounting for over 90% of reported cases worldwide [5,6]. During the period from 2004 to 2019, a total of 209,209 cases of HFRS were reported, with a case fatality rate(CFR) of 0.89% [7]. In recent years, there has been a coexistence of multiple HVs gene branches [8], an expanding epidemic area, an 8236120472 to XQL], Jiangxi Provincial Youth Science Foundation [grant 20171BAB215051 to TCZ], Jiangxi Provincial Natural Science Foundation [grant 20242BAB25552 to TCZ], Jiangxi Provincial Key Laboratory of Major Epidemic Prevention and Control [grant 2024SSY06021], and Science and Technology Program of Jiangxi Provincial Health Commission [grant 202610833 to GHX]. The domestic HFRS epidemic sources are mainly distributed in plains and hilly areas with an altitude of less than 500 meters, areas with abundant water in temperate and subtropical monsoon climate zones, and regions where wet animals are geographically distributed [11]. Jiangxi is a high-incidence area for HFRS in China and is characterized by the co-circulation of both HTNV and SEOV [12,13]. During 2005 and 2024, almost 10,000 HFRS cases were reported, with a CFR of 1.1%. Furthermore, the disease was reported in over 90% of all counties and districts. Previous studies have found that the incidence of HFRS in Jiangxi Province shows spatial clustering [14]. HFRS cases are concentrated in the Chiu-ling Mountains and then spread to the Wuyi Mountain hills over time, and three clusters were detected [12]. The Cluster I, situated in the northwestern region between the Chiu-ling Mountains and the western side of Poyang Lake, represents a historical high-incidence area (aver­ age annual rate: 12.10 per 100,000) [12]. In contrast, The Clusters II and III, located to the east and south of Poyang Lake and within the Wuyi Mountains region, exhibited progressively lower incidence rates of 4.20 and 1.80 per 100,000, respec­ tively [12]. HTNV strains in Jiangxi were in one independent branch, while the SEOV strains in Jiangxi were relatively more diverse [13]. Laboratory evidence from one county in Cluster I indicated the exclusive presence of HTNV and the absence of SEOV [15]. The distinctive spatial patterning of HFRS in Jiangxi Province may be related to two primary factors. First, natural bar­ riers, including mountain ranges and Poyang Lake, likely restrict host movement and viral gene flow among the different clusters [16,17]. Second, variations in altitude contribute to divergent ecological niches for reservoir rodent species [18]. Building on the observed correlation between spatial distribution and incidence rates, we hypothesize that: (1) in high- incidence areas, residents tended to have shorter onset-to-visit intervals, and local health facilities had more extensive experience in the diagnosis and treatment of the disease; and (2) influenced by this spatial and environmental hetero­ geneity, the prevalence of SEOV and HTNV, as well as the host carriage rates, may vary, with potential implications for differences in disease severity across populations. To test these hypotheses, we conducted a retrospective study investi­ gating the clinical severity and the healthcare-seeking behaviors of HFRS cases. Materials and methods Ethics statement This study was based on data collected through routine epidemiological investigations conducted by county-level CDC professionals as part of the statutory notifiable infectious disease surveillance system in Jiangxi Province, China. The study was reviewed and approved by the Ethics Review Committee of Jiangxi Provincial Center for Disease Control and Prevention (approval number: Gan CDC Ke Lun Shen (2025) No. 04). The requirement for informed consent was waived because the data were derived from routine statutory surveillance and the study posed no additional risk to subjects, in accordance with Chinese regulations governing the use of statutory communicable disease surveillance data for public health purposes. Study area Jiangxi is located in south eastern China (24°29′14′′–30°04′44′′N, 113°34′36′′–118°28′58′′E), a humid subtropical climate area that includes 11 cities and 100 counties. It is surrounded by mountains on the east, south and west sides, with exten­ sive hills in the inner area and a vast plain in the north and central parts [19]. The southern part of the province is hills with ranges and valleys interlaced; while the central and northern parts have a relatively flat terrain with lower altitudes. The entire province extends from south to north, tilting towards Poyang Lake, which forms a huge basin, with an open area to the north [19]. Previous spatial analyses [12] have identified three distinct clusters of HFRS cases in Jiangxi Province (S1 Text). The Cluster I is located on the west side of the northern hilly area and includes some plain counties adjacent to PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pntd.0014746 September 23, 2026 4 / 17 rivers and lakes. The Cluster II areas is located on the east side of the northern hilly area. The Cluster III is located on the south side of the northern hilly area, and also includes some plain counties adjacent to rivers and lakes. The Cluster II and Cluster III are both close to the Wuyi Mountains, and the Cluster III borders the Cluster I. Epidemiological investigations In accordance with the National Surveillance Program for Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome, epidemiological investigations were promptly initiated by trained professionals from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention after hospital notification of HFRS cases — including both clinically diagnosed and laboratory-confirmed cases as defined by the WS278–2008 criteria (S2 Text) —using the nationally standardized HFRS case investigation questionnaire to obtain field information (S3 Text) on general patient characteristics, laboratory diagnosis situation, clinical severity, and healthcare-seeking behaviors with supplementary telephone interviews conducted when necessary. Personal and healthcare-access details were provided by patients themselves or by family members when the patient was unable to communicate—for example, due to death, severe illness, or young age. Clinical information was obtained by consulting treating physicians and reviewing medical records. Based on the clinical characteristics, HFRS severity was divided into four clinical types (S4 Text): mild (renal injury without hypotension or oliguria), moderate (uremia with acute renal failure and oliguria), severe (hypotension with severe uremia and oliguria), and critical (refractory shock, organ failure, or severe renal failure). Severity classification was determined by attending physicians for surviving patients based on the above standardized criteria at the time of admission. Study participants A total of 7,172 cases were reported during the study period from 2011 to 2023. As the national surveillance program did not mandate case-based investigation for all counties, 2,374(33.10%) cases lacked standardized epidemiological data. Among the remaining 4,798(66.90%) cases included for initial review, we performed detailed verification and excluded those with logical error (visit date later than onset date; age inconsistent with reported occupation) or lack of key infor­ mation (age, gender, current address, visit date and onset date). Consequently, 4,614(64.33%, 4,614/7,172) cases were included in the final analysis, with 2,320 cases in Cluster I, 1,120 cases in Cluster II, 542 cases in Cluster III, and 632 cases in non-clustered areas (Fig 1). The included cases (4,614) were largely comparable to all reported cases (7,172) in terms of gender, age, and main occupational composition, and their epidemic trends were also highly similar (S1 Fig). Fur­ thermore, the included (4,614) and excluded (2,558) cases exhibited similar age and gender distributions, suggesting that selection bias was limited (S2 Fig). Collectively, these findings indicate that the analytic sample was highly representative. Statistical analysis Differences across clusters were compared using the Kruskal-Wallis H test for continuous variables, and the Chi-square or Fisher’s exact test for categorical variables. Post-hoc pairwise comparisons were performed with Bonferroni correction when global tests were significant. To adjust for potential confounders, two separate multivariable logistic regression models were constructed: one for clinical severity (mild/moderate vs. severe/critical) and one for hospital level (Class II vs. Class III/III+), with cluster, age, sex, occupation, and year of onset as covariates. Adjusted odds ratios (aORs) with 95% CIs were reported. All statistical analyses were conducted using R software (version 4.3.0), and a P < 0.05 was considered to be significant. Results Patients’ general characteristics From 2011 to 2023, a total of 7,172 cases were reported in Jiangxi Province, corresponding to a cumulative incidence rate of 1.64 per 100,000 population. The annual reported incidence rate showed an overall downward trend (S3 Fig), declining PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pntd.0014746 September 23, 2026 5 / 17 with fluctuations from 1.24 per 100,000 in 2011 to 0.66 per 100,000 in 2023. Substantial variation in cumulative incidence was observed across clusters: the rates were 7.50, 3.27, and 1.46 per 100,000 for Clusters I, II and III, respectively, com­ pared with 0.34 per 100,000 in the non‐clustered areas. Among the 4,614 analyzed cases, the male-to-female ratio was 2.09:1 (3,123 vs. 1,491), which did not differ significantly across the four areas. The mean age was 49 ± 18 years. The pro­ portion of cases in the 0–20 age group was significantly higher in Cluster I (14.44%) than in other areas (4.59% ~ 6.46%), whereas the opposite trend was observed for the 41–60 age group (37.20% vs. 46.25% ~ 49.45%). Funding: This work was supported by the Natural Science Foundation of China [grant RESEARCH ARTICLE Clinical severity and health-seeking behaviors of cases with hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome: A comparative study across spatial clusters in Jiangxi Province, China Guanghui Xia1, Rui Gao2, Huanhong Pan1, Jun Zong1, Zhili Zeng1, Zifen Li1, Chenwei Li1, Shiyu Liao2, Tong Luo1, Guai Tang1, Zijing Peng2, Xiaoqing Liu1, Shiwen Liu1, Jianxiong Li1, Tianchen Zhang 1* 1 Jiangxi Provincial Key Laboratory of Major Epidemics Prevention and Control/ Medical Leading Discipline of Jiangxi Province (Epidemiology), Jiangxi Provincial Center for Disease Control and Prevention, Nanchang, Jiangxi, China, 2 School of Public Health, Jiangxi Medical College, Nanchang University/ Jiangxi Provincial Key Laboratory of Disease Prevention and Public Health, Nanchang University, Nanchang, Jiangxi, China * jorangezhang@163.com Abstract Background Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a significant public health concern in Jiangxi Province, China, where both Hantaan (HTNV) and Seoul (SEOV) co- circulate. Previous studies have identified three distinct clusters of HFRS epidemic in Jiangxi Province, characterized by geographical separation and heterogeneous incidence levels. We hypothesized that clinical severity and healthcare-seeking behaviors may vary across these clusters, and thus conducted a retrospective study to examine this hypothesis. Methods We retrospectively analyzed 4,614 HFRS cases (13-year period) from 63 counties. Cases were classified into four areas based on prior spatial study, representing distinct hilly and plain regions with different proximity to major water bodies and mountains. Data on HFRS cases were collected by county-level CDC staff using a nationally standardized case investigation questionnaire. Clinical severity and healthcare-seeking behaviors (hospital level, onset-to-visit interval) were compared. Results HFRS cases in Cluster I exhibited the highest clinical severity (22.41% severe, 6.65% critical), while cases in Cluster II were strikingly mild (2.62% severe, 1.31% critical). Median onset-to-visit interval was longest in Cluster II (5 days) vs others (2–4 days). Hospital preference varied: Cluster I primarily used Class II hospitals (65.88%); PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pntd.0014746 September 23, 2026 2 / 17 Cluster II showed near-equal use of Class II (48.44%) and III (47.01%); Cluster III and non-clustered areas favored higher-level hospitals. Conclusion Our findings confirmed that Jiangxi Province, though a mixed epidemic focus, exhib­ ited distinct spatial heterogeneity in clinical severity, and healthcare-seeking behav­ iors. These findings underscore the need for regionally tailored strategies in HFRS prevention and control. Author summary Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a serious infectious disease in China, with thousands of cases reported annually. Previous studies have shown that cases in Jiangxi Province tend to cluster in specific geographic areas. How­ ever, it remained unclear whether patients in these different areas experienced different disease outcomes or sought care in different ways. In this study, we analyzed data from more than 4,600 patients across 63 counties over 13 years. We found that disease severity and how quickly people sought care differed sub­ stantially between regions. Patients in Cluster I were much more likely to devel­ op severe or critical illness, whereas cases in Cluster II were predominantly mild. We also identified significant inter-regional differences in healthcare-seeking behavior, including time to initial care and choice of healthcare facility. Cluster I patients predominantly utilized Class II hospitals, while those in other regions more often presented directly to Class III hospitals. These findings show that HFRS affects different parts of Jiangxi Province in different ways. This means that public health strategies—such as health education campaigns and hospital resource planning—should be tailored to the specific needs of each region, rath­ er than using a one-size-fits-all approach. papers.title: The efficacy of Cordyceps sinensis preparations in improving kidney outcomes among patients with AKI during hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome: evidence from a Chinese cohort
papers.abstract: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is frequently complicated by acute kidney injury (AKI). Although most patients recover from AKI with supportive care, some progress to chronic kidney disease (CKD). The incidence and determinants of CKD progression in patients with HFRS-AKI remain uncertain. Here, 99 patients with HFRS-AKI treated at Jinling Hospital were analyzed retrospectively to determine the rate of CKD progression and identify associated risk factors. Patients were divided into complete recovery (CR) and incomplete recovery (ICR) groups according to CKD progression. Baseline clinical and laboratory data were collected and analyzed. Overall, 27.3% of patients with HFRS-AKI progressed to CKD despite receiving supportive care. Facial flushing was more frequent in the ICR group than in the CR group (40.7% vs. 18.1%, p = 0.033). Multivariate analysis revealed that treatment with Cordyceps sinensis preparations during the AKI phase was an independent protective factor against incomplete kidney recovery (OR: 0.323, 95% CI: 0.114–0.916, p = 0.034). Inverse probability weighting analysis further demonstrated that the use of Cordyceps sinensis preparations was inversely associated with incomplete kidney recovery (β: −1.184, 95% CI: −2.224 – −0.144, p = 0.026). Survival analysis confirmed that Cordyceps sinensis preparation therapy was associated with improved kidney outcomes (log-rank test, p = 0.004). This study provides the first clinical evidence that adjunctive therapy with Cordyceps sinensis preparations during HFRS-AKI is associated with improved kidney outcomes, suggesting that Cordyceps sinensis preparations represents a promising therapeutic approach for viral-induced AKI.

analysis.background: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is frequently complicated by acute kidney injury (AKI), and some patients progress to chronic kidney disease (CKD), representing a significant clinical concern.
analysis.methods: A retrospective cohort of 99 HFRS‑AKI patients treated at Jinling Hospital was analyzed; patients were divided into complete recovery (CR) and incomplete recovery (ICR) groups and baseline clinical and laboratory data were collected.
analysis.results: Overall, 27.3% of patients progressed to CKD; treatment with Cordyceps sinensis preparations was an independent protective factor against incomplete recovery (OR 0.323, 95% CI 0.114–0.916, p = 0.034), inverse probability weighting showed β = −1.184 (95% CI −2.224 to −0.144, p = 0.026), and survival analysis confirmed improved kidney outcomes (log‑rank p = 0.004).
analysis.contribution: This study provides the first clinical evidence that adjunctive Cordyceps sinensis therapy during HFRS‑AKI is associated with improved renal outcomes, suggesting a promising therapeutic approach for viral‑induced AKI.
analysis.limitations: Only an abstract is available, so detailed methodology, full sample characteristics, and potential confounders are not reported.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome often leads to AKI and can progress to CKD, a major health issue. Methods: A retrospective analysis of 99 HFRS‑AKI patients at Jinling Hospital classified them into complete or incomplete recovery groups and collected baseline data. Results: 27.3% progressed to CKD; Cordyceps sinensis use reduced incomplete recovery risk (OR 0.323, 95% CI 0.114–0.916, p = 0.034), with supportive inverse probability weighting (β = −1.184, p = 0.026) and survival analysis (log‑rank p = 0.004). Contribution: First clinical evidence that Cordyceps sinensis adjunct therapy improves kidney outcomes in viral‑induced AKI. Limitations: Only abstract data are available, limiting detail on methods and confounders.

papers.title: Hantavirus preparedness at human-rodent interfaces: lessons from China's HFRS control and Andes virus transmission in mobile populations.
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses are globally distributed reservoir-associated viruses that cause haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), mainly in Eurasia, and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS; also termed hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, HPS), mainly in the Americas. Most human infections arise from exposure to rodent-contaminated environments, so clustered disease may reflect shared environmental exposure rather than interpersonal transmission. This Review uses China's long-term HFRS experience as a central case study for interface-centred preparedness. China demonstrates that sustained surveillance, reservoir monitoring, risk-defined vaccination, rodent control and environmental risk reduction can substantially reduce disease burden, but declining incidence does not mean disappearance of ecological risk. Its dual HTNV and SEOV ecology further shows that one clinical syndrome can arise from distinct agricultural and peri-domestic rat-associated interfaces. Andes virus (ANDV) provides a contrasting challenge: selected outbreaks have documented limited but consequential human-to-human transmission after close or prolonged contact. The 2026 MV Hondius event illustrates how such transmission can become an international contact-tracing problem when it occurs in mobile populations. Preparedness should therefore combine long-term management of rodent-derived interfaces, rapid discrimination between common-source clusters and ANDV secondary transmission, and response systems that remain effective when exposed persons, infected animals or close contacts cross geographical borders.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are globally distributed reservoir‑associated viruses that cause haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in Eurasia and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS/HPS) in the Americas, with most human infections arising from exposure to rodent‑contaminated environments.
analysis.main_directions: The review focuses on China’s long‑term HFRS control (surveillance, reservoir monitoring, risk‑defined vaccination, rodent control, environmental risk reduction) and contrasts it with Andes virus (ANDV) outbreaks that can involve limited but consequential human‑to‑human transmission in mobile populations.
analysis.current_state: China’s integrated approach has substantially reduced disease burden, yet declining incidence does not eliminate ecological risk, and the dual HTNV and SEOV ecology shows that one clinical syndrome can stem from distinct agricultural and peri‑domestic rat‑associated interfaces.
analysis.gaps: The 2026 MV Hondius event illustrates how ANDV transmission can become an international contact‑tracing problem, revealing limited data on rapid discrimination between common‑source clusters and secondary human‑to‑human spread.
analysis.future_research: Preparedness should incorporate rapid field diagnostics and coordinated cross‑border tracing systems that remain effective when infected persons, animals, or close contacts move across geographical borders.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses cause HFRS in Eurasia and HCPS/HPS in the Americas, with most cases from rodent‑contaminated environments. Main directions: The review examines China’s integrated HFRS control (surveillance, vaccination, rodent control) and contrasts it with Andes virus outbreaks that can involve limited human‑to‑human spread in mobile groups. Current state: China’s approach has markedly lowered disease burden, yet ecological risk persists, and dual HTNV/SEOV cycles show distinct agricultural versus peri‑domestic interfaces. Gaps: The 2026 MV Hondius event highlights the challenge of cross‑border transmission and limited data on distinguishing common‑source from secondary cases. Future research: Develop rapid diagnostics and coordinated international tracing systems that function when infected persons, animals, or contacts cross regions.

papers.title_zh: 汉坦病毒 人-鼠界面的防备:来自中国肾综合征出血热防控的经验以及 安第斯病毒 在流动人群中的传播。

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒es 是全球分布的与宿主相关的病毒,导致欧亚地区的肾综合征出血热 (HFRS) 和美洲的 汉坦病毒心肺综合征(HCPS/HPS),大多数人类感染源于接触受鼠类污染的环境。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 本综述聚焦中国长期的肾综合征出血热控制(监测、宿主监控、风险导向的疫苗接种、鼠类控制、环境风险降低),并将其与 安第斯病毒(ANDV)暴发进行对比,后者在流动人群中可能出现有限但有重要影响的人际传播。
analysis_zh.current_state: 中国的综合防控措施已显著降低疾病负担,但发病率下降并未消除生态风险,HTNV 与 SEOV 的双重生态表明,同一种临床综合征可源自不同的农业和居家周边鼠类关联环境。
analysis_zh.gaps: 2026 年 MV Hondius 事件展示了 ANDV 传播如何演变为国际接触追踪难题,暴露出在快速区分共同来源聚集与二次人际传播方面数据有限。
analysis_zh.future_research: 应急准备应纳入快速现场诊断和协同的跨境追踪体系,以在感染者、动物或密切接触者跨越地理边界时仍保持有效。

papers.title: Immunopathogenesis of vascular leakage in hantavirus infections: a systematic review of mechanisms underlying HPS and HFRS
papers.abstract: Hantavirus infections manifest as Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (HPS) and Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS), both associated with increased vascular permeability despite the lack of direct cytopathic injury to endothelial cells. A systematic search of PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science (January 2020–May 2026) identified human studies investigating immunopathogenic mechanisms in HPS or HFRS. Due to substantial heterogeneity across study designs, findings were synthesized descriptively. Forty-one studies (39 cohorts, 2 case–control) were included, predominantly on HFRS-associated hantaviruses (HTNV, PUUV, DOBV); only one study evaluated HPS-associated ANDV. The reviewed literature revealed elevated inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-18, CXCL10, CX3CL1), depletion of Mucosal-Associated Invariant T (MAIT) cells linked to IRE1αdependent pyroptosis, disruption of the endothelial glycocalyx, and coagulation disturbances with platelet dysfunction. Biomarkers of glycocalyx injury (heparan sulfate, chondroitin sulfate, and soluble thrombomodulin) were associated with increased mortality risk (AUC 0.87–0.93). No human mechanistic studies on Sin Nombre virus (SNV) were identified. Hantavirus-induced vascular leakage is driven by cytokine-mediated endothelial dysfunction, MAIT cell pyroptosis, glycocalyx degradation, and immunothrombosis. While HFRS mechanisms are now well-characterized, the absence of human mechanistic data for HPS—particularly for SNV—remains a critical gap.

papers.title: Revisiting Animal Reservoirs of Hantavirus and Other Zoonotic Viruses Associated with Cruise Travel: Impact and Prevention.
papers.abstract: The sustained growth of international maritime tourism and the expansion of the cruise industry have increased the importance of emerging zoonotic diseases as a significant challenge to global public health. Cruise ships constitute complex epidemiological settings characterized by high population density, rapid international mobility, and constant interaction between humans, animals, and coastal environments, factors that favor the introduction and spread of emerging infectious agents. Potential zoonotic concerns include orthohantaviruses and other zoonotic viruses, such as dengue, chikungunya, Zika, yellow fever, and avian influenza, which are associated with animal reservoirs and vectors in ports, tourist destinations, and tropical ecosystems. This review examines the ecology of animal reservoirs of orthohantaviruses and other zoonotic pathogens relevant to maritime tourism, including peri-urban rodents, bats, migratory birds, and other mammals. It discusses how climate change, coastal urbanization, and environmental change affect viral transmission dynamics. It highlights epidemiological risks linked to international cruises, particularly exposure during ecotourism excursions, pathogen introduction, and challenges for maritime surveillance. The review also addresses travel medicine, biosecurity, and infection control, emphasizing a One Health approach. Strengthening integrated surveillance and prevention systems is essential to ensure safer, more sustainable, and resilient maritime tourism in the 21st century.

papers.title_zh: 重新审视与邮轮旅行相关的 汉坦病毒 及其他人畜共患病毒的动物宿主:影响与防控。

analysis_zh.background: 国际邮轮旅游的快速扩张提升了新发人畜共患疾病的风险,促使对与海上旅行相关的动物宿主进行审查。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 本综述概述了邮轮的独特流行病学环境、与啮齿动物、蝙蝠、候鸟及其他哺乳动物相关的多种人畜共患病毒(正汉坦病毒es、登革热、基孔肯雅热、寨卡病毒、黄热病、禽流感),以及气候变化和沿海城市化对传播的影响。
analysis_zh.current_state: 现有认识表明,这些宿主和媒介在港口及旅游目的地是旅行者感染的来源,并已有文献记录其在短途旅行中可能引入病原体。
analysis_zh.gaps: 船舶和港口的监测空白及生物安全挑战限制了对引入病原体的检测和控制。
analysis_zh.future_research: 需要加强综合“一体化健康”监测、气候影响研究以及针对性的感染控制措施,以提升海上旅游的安全性和韧性。

papers.title: Differences in Ecological Drivers for Leptospira and Hantavirus in an Urban Norway Rat Population.
papers.abstract: Rodent control in urban areas is an important public health measure, among other reasons, for their capacity of harboring several zoonotic pathogens. Efficient, evidence-based control programs must consider both rodent and pathogen ecology, to achieve both rodent population and pathogen transmission risk reduction. The present study aims to determine the ecological drivers of Leptospira and Hantavirus positivity in an urban Norway Rat population. One hundred and twenty rats were trapped in four urban poor communities in Salvador, Brazil, tested for Leptospira sp. and Hantavirus. Generalized Linear Models for Leptospira (N=109) and Hantavirus (N=108) positivity were created with a pool of environmental and demographic variables, followed by stepwise model selection using Akaike's Information Criterion. Age, presence of Calodium hepaticum scars, wounds, accumulated materials, open sewer canals and unpaved soil were positively associated with Leptospira positivity. Age and presence of accumulated materials were positively associated with Hantavirus positivity, while rodent control campaigns and being male were protective factors. Factors associated with positivity for Leptospira are also associated with rodent infestation. Different subsets of environmental and demographic factors influence pathogens with different epidemiological characteristics. Control measures that effectively reduce zoonotic risk must consider the ecological characteristics of the pathogens present in the system.
authors: Ana Maria Borges da Paixão Barreto
