Keywords: Rattus norvegicus, Hantavirus, Leptospira, environmental conditions, neglected tropical disease INTRODUCTION Old world rats (genus Rattus) are the most ubiquitous synanthropic animals. Their global distribution and occurrence arise from their intimate relationship with hu- man presence, following major human movements throughout the globe, such as the Transatlantic navigation and the Silk Route (Morand et al. 2015). Currently, rats are almost exclusively associated with human occupation, often of urbanized areas, are significantly dependent on the re- sources made available by human activity (Feng and Himsworth 2013). The relationship between rats and humans is not harmonious, with rats being considered pests, causing damage to farming and infrastructure, and contaminating food stocks (Jacob and Buckle 2018). Estimations suggest, conservatively, that the Norway rat, Rattus norvegicus, alone causes economic damage of more than USD 30 million/ year globally (Diagne et al. 2023). Throughout the Global South, the fast growth of urban centers often results in the creation of informal settlements, characterized by deficiencies in the provision and coverage of basic urban services (e.g., trash collection, sanitation, pest control) and infrastructure (Carvalho-Pereira et al. 2024; Costa et al. 2014; de Oliveira et al. 2024). The resulting environment is highly conductive to rodent infestation, with an abundance of water, food and shelter (Panti-May et al. 2016). Such close coexistence exposes the populations of the settlements to the pathogens carried by rats (Costa, Ribeiro, et al. 2014; Muschetto et al. 2025). The role of rats as a zoonotic pathogen reservoir is arguably one of the most impactful threats posed by our proximity. Rodents host a remarkable diversity of zoonotic pathogens, including viruses, bacteria, unicellular eukary- ote and helminth parasites (Luis et al. 2013; Himsworth et al. 2013; Delaney, Treuting, and Rothenburger 2018). Some of the most historically relevant pathogens have ro- dents as their reservoir, such as Yersinia pestis (Rahelinirina et al. 2021), Leptospira sp. (A. Minter et al. 2017) and Hantavirus (Dearing and Dizney 2010). Depending on the pathogen, rodents can either be direct sources of infection or act as part of the transmission cycle, shedding bacteria to the environment or promoting infective contact with competent hosts that thus infect humans (Himsworth et al. 2013). Important examples of pathogens carried by Norway rats are Leptospira spp. (Feng and Himsworth 2013), Hantavirus (Chen et al. 2023), and Toxoplasma gondii (Bazan et al. 2025). Leptospira spp., the causative agent of leptospirosis, is a genus of bacteria transmitted by water and soil contaminated by the urine of infected hosts such as rats, which are asymptomatic carriers and chronic shedders of the bacteria (Guerra 2009; Tucunduva de Faria et al. 2007). With over one million estimated human cases per year (Costa et al. 2015), the infection can cause asymptomatic/mild forms or evolve into severe and potentially lethal forms such as Weil’s disease and Leptospirosis-associated pulmonary hemor- rhage syndrome (Ko, Goarant, and Picardeau 2009). In Salvador, leptospirosis is a long-standing challenge to public health in impoverished urban communities (Ko et al. 1999; Ribeiro et al. 2008). Hantavirus (Hantaviridae: genus Orthohantavirus) is a genus of negative-sense RNA viruses maintained mainly by small mammals (Bradfute et al. 2024), with several species pathogenic to humans. The clade is divided in Old World Hantaviruses (e.g., Orthohantavirus seoulense [SEOV], Orthohantavirus hantanense [HTNV]), causative agents of Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome, and New World Hantaviruses (e.g., Orthohantavirus andense [ANDV], Orthohantavirus sinnombreense [SNV]), causative agents of Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (Chen et al. 2023). Norway rats are the main reservoirs of Orthohantavirus seoulense, with chronic, nearly asymptomatic infection (Jonsson et al.2010; Meyer and Schmaljohn 2000). SEOV is considered to be cosmopolitan following the worldwide distribution of rats (Himsworth et al. 2013) and has been previously detected in rats in Salvador (Costa et al. 2014). Toxoplasma gondii is an apicomplexan parasite that widely infects warm-blooded animals, causing grave illness in immunocompromised individuals, as well as fetal development issues through congenital toxoplasmosis (S.G. C. G. Zeppelini et al. Sanchez and Besteiro 2021). While important for the epi- demiology of toxoplasmosis, infection by T. gondii in rats causes behavioral changes, but limited health effects (Ruf- folo et al. 2016; Webster 1994). For the control of rat-borne zoonoses, the ecology of the zoonotic system should also be considered, as this presents its own ecological characteristics (Caio et al. 2016), an important consideration given the diversity of patho- gens that rats can carry, including potential coinfections (Carvalho-Pereira et al. 2018; Costa et al. 2014; L.K.F. Lee et al. 2023). Previous studies in urban informal settlements in Salvador have investigated urban rodent ecology (Panti- May et al. 2016; C. G. Zeppelini et al. 2021; Eyre et al. 2020), movement (Awoniyi et al. 2021), the parasites and pathogens they carry (Costa, Porter, et al. 2014; Carvalho- Pereira et al. 2018), and the impacts of infestation on hu- man health (Costa, Ribeiro, et al. 2014; Costa et al. 2021). However, studies have focused on isolated pathogens (Souza et al. 2021; Bazan et al. 2025; Pimentel Sobrinho et al. 2020), not yet evaluating potential ecological inter- actions between these pathogens, such as how environ- mental and demographic factors might differ between them. Knowledge of pathogen ecology of Norway rats, a multi-pathogen reservoir, including prevalence and pa- thogen characteristics and the impacts of environmental factors on their dynamics is essential to lead to targeted control and intervention strategies. Different pathogens can present different characteristics (e.g., acquisition route, tissue tropism, requirements for transmission) even if infecting the same host species, likely resulting in different responses to control measures. Our study aims to quantify zoonotic positivity for three different pathogens (Hantavirus, Leptospira spp. and Toxoplasma gondii) in Norway rats from urban impover- ished communities in the city of Salvador, Bahia, Brazil, and identify whether the ecological processes that drive rat infection risk vary between pathogens. Characterizing zoonotic spillover risk in rodents and identifying environ- mental risk factors is fundamental for the development of rodent-borne zoonosis control programs that are resilient against the risk of pathogen (re)emergence as an unpre- dicted negative effect of the control program itself. MATERIALS AND METHODS Ethical Statement Rodent sampling and biological sample harvesting proce- dures were authorized under license from the Ethics Committee for Animal Use of Fiocruz Bahia (authorization #019/2016). The study was conducted and reported fol- lowing ARRIVE guidelines. Study Site The city of Salvador, Bahia (12 550 28.03‘‘ S, 38 280 34.900 W) is one of the largest urban centers in Brazil, with 692,819 km2 and over 2.5 million inhabitants, 42.7% of which living in informal settlements (henceforth commu- nities) (IBGE 2022, 2015). Four communities were sam- pled: Marechal Rondon (MR), Alto do Cabrito (AC), Rio Sena (RS) e Nova Constituinte (NC), selected for their location in the same sanitary district (subdivisions of the city’s territory used for the operations of health authorities, including the Zoonosis Control Center [CCZ]), reflecting their sociodemographic similarity and environmental pro- file, which fit the criteria for classification as slums (inad- equate housing conditions, limited or absent access to safe drinking water and sanitation), (Economic and Affairs 2019), and lack of adequate solid waste collection (in- cluding formation of open trash piles). All four commu- nities were set on hills, with small natural waterways running at their lowermost point, which receive the com- munities’ household sewage. According to the CCZ, the communities have chronic issues with rodent infestation. In each community, the study area was defined as a poly- gon of 0.07–0.09 km2. Zoonotic Positivity for Rattus Norvegicus Rat capture data, and environmental and biological sam- ples (kidney imprints, urine, blood and brain matter) were obtained from a previous field sampling study conducted in four communities, performed in two campaigns (40 semi- randomized trapping points with two Tomahawk-type traps, 4 trap-nights per campaign, April-June and October– November 2018) (C. G. Zeppelini et al. 2021). During necropsy and tissue sample harvesting, the presence of Calodium hepaticum (a helminth species that parasitises the liver of mammals, frequently observed in wild Rattus) was registered during the examination of the liver. The presence Differences in Ecological Drivers for Leptospira and Hantavirus of the characteristic scars in the liver cortex was considered as a positive detection for the individual (Fuehrer 2014). Positivity for Leptospira was assessed by a combination of Indirect Fluorescent Antibody (IFA) assays performed on Poli-L-Lysine-treated microscope slides with kidney imprints (D et al. 2016) and/or urine sample qPCR tar- geting the lipL32 gene as previously described (Costa, Wunder, et al. 2015). Hantavirus positivity was determined by Enzyme-linked Immunoassay (ELISA) tests, using orthohantavirus purified recombinant nucleoprotein as antigen (Padula et al. 2000). Detection of Toxoplasma was performed through nested-PCR tests targeting the IST1 region of T. gondii (Hurtado et al. 2001). Due to limitations in availability, PCR tests for Hantavirus (RT-PCR targeting the Hantavirus-specific RNA-dependent RNA polymerase- encoding L segment) were restricted to ELISA-positive rats. All PCR tests were negative. The physical condition of rats was measured as a weight-length ratio that took into account the effect of age (Peig and Green 2009). Age of individuals was calculated in days based in morphometric data following the von Ber- talanffy equation, with parameters obtained by fitting data derived from the growth curve for male rats (Calhoun 1962; Burthe et al. 2009). Morphology data, presence of parasites and of wounds were obtained during animal processing (C. G. Zeppelini et al. 2021). Environmental Variables A standardized descriptive questionnaire was applied to obtain the environmental data used to characterize the environment at each sampling point. The data collection occurred at the moment of trapping, being performed considering a 20-m-radius buffer around the sampling point (C. G. Zeppelini et al. 2021). Variables describe the presence of other animals, human-made materials (refuse, construction materials, debris), soil condition and presence of water, as well as rodent control activities (both carried by the locals themselves and by the Zoonosis Control Center) in the region at the moment the traps were set. Data on opossum presence were derived from captures during the trapping period. Data on presence of animals and rodent control measures in the trapping area (i.e., household backyards) were voluntarily provided by the resident dur- ing trap setting. Variables collected are listed in Table 1. Statistical Analysis To evaluate each outcome (positivity for Leptospira, Tox- oplasma, or Hantavirus), a set of variables was defined based on hypotheses that link the biological processes known to be relevant to each pathogen to the outcome (Table 1). Positivity for the other pathogens was also added as a variable to evaluate if coinfection affects the chances of positivity for each zoonotic pathogen. Collinearity was verified through the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF), with variables having a VIF under 5 considered apt to compose the variable pool for each outcome. Generalized linear models (GLMs) were performed for each outcome using the VIF-verified and hypothesis-associated variables, fol- lowed by backwards stepwise model selection based on the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC). Models were consid- ered plausible when DAIC < 2 compared to the model with the lowest AIC and selected based on maximum parsimony (lowest DAIC and number of variables). All analyses were performed using the packages Tidyverse, lme4 e MuMIn, on R Core Team, 2026 (Wickham et al. 2019; Bates et al. 2015; Barton 2022). RESULTS Zoonotic Positivity for Rattus Norvegicus One-hundred and sixteen individuals were tested for Lep- tospira, with 48.3% positivity (56/116); 117 tested for Hantavirus with 31.6% positivity (37/117) and 9 samples with indeterminate status; and 120 tested for Toxoplasma, with 2.5% positivity (3/120). Due to the low positivity for Toxoplasma, only Hantavirus and Leptospira were analysed by GLM and model selection. The model for Leptospira was performed with 109 individuals (7 individuals removed due to incomplete associated data), with this subset presenting 48.6% (53/ 109) positivity, and 108 individuals were employed for the Hantavirus model (9 individuals removed due to incom- plete data), presenting 33.3% (36/108) positivity. From the subsets with complete data, 39.6% (21/53) of the Lep- tospira-positive rats were also positive for Hantavirus, while 58.3% (21/36) of orthohantavirus-positive rats were also positive for Leptospira. C. G. Zeppelini et al. Leptospira Positivity Model Fifty-six models were considered plausible (DAIC <2) after model selection. Among the plausible models, five were equally parsimonious (four variables each), contain- ing six variables between them. These six variables were age estimated in days (present in 49/56 plausible models), presence of Calodium hepaticum scars in the liver (50/56), presence of open sewers within a 20-m-radius buffer (37/ 56), the presence of accumulated materials (45/56), type of ground cover (54/56), and presence of wounds (56/56) (for the full model selection table, see Appendix S1: Table S1). Bara ̃o do Geremoabo, 147, Salvador, Brazil 9Programa de Po ́s-Graduac ̧a ̃o em Ecologia: Teoria, Aplicac ̧o ̃es e Valores, Universidade Federal da Bahia, R. Bara ̃o do Geremoabo, 147, Salvador, Brazil 10London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, Keppel Street, London WC1E 7HT, UK 11Yale School of Public Health, 60 College St, New Haven, CT 06510 12Department of Evolution, Ecology and Behaviour, University of Liverpool, Biosciences Building, Liverpool L69 7ZB, UK Abstract: Rodent control in urban areas is an important public health measure, among other reasons, for their capacity of harboring several zoonotic pathogens. Efficient, evidence-based control programs must consider both rodent and pathogen ecology, to achieve both rodent population and pathogen transmission risk reduction. The present study aims to determine the ecological drivers of Leptospira and Hantavirus positivity in an urban Norway Rat population. One hundred and twenty rats were trapped in four urban poor communities in Salvador, Brazil, tested for Leptospira sp. and Hantavirus. Generalized Linear Models for Leptospira (N=109) and Hantavirus (N=108) positivity were created with a pool of environmental and demographic variables, followed by stepwise model selection using Akaike’s Information Criterion. Age, presence of Calodium hep- aticum scars, wounds, accumulated materials, open sewer canals and unpaved soil were positively associated with Leptospira positivity. Age and presence of accumulated materials were positively associated with Han- tavirus positivity, while rodent control campaigns and being male were protective factors. Factors associated with positivity for Leptospira are also associated with rodent infestation. Different subsets of environmental and Correspondence to: Caio G. Zeppelini, e-mail: czeppelini@gmail.com EcoHealth https://doi.org/10.1007/s10393-026-01836-z  2026 The Author(s) demographic factors influence pathogens with different epidemiological characteristics. Control measures that effectively reduce zoonotic risk must consider the ecological characteristics of the pathogens present in the system. Keywords: Rattus norvegicus, Hantavirus, Leptospira, environmental conditions, neglected tropical disease INTRODUCTION Old world rats (genus Rattus) are the most ubiquitous synanthropic animals. Their global distribution and occurrence arise from their intimate relationship with hu- man presence, following major human movements throughout the globe, such as the Transatlantic navigation and the Silk Route (Morand et al. 2015). Currently, rats are almost exclusively associated with human occupation, often of urbanized areas, are significantly dependent on the re- sources made available by human activity (Feng and Himsworth 2013). The relationship between rats and humans is not harmonious, with rats being considered pests, causing damage to farming and infrastructure, and contaminating food stocks (Jacob and Buckle 2018). Estimations suggest, conservatively, that the Norway rat, Rattus norvegicus, alone causes economic damage of more than USD 30 million/ year globally (Diagne et al. 2023). Throughout the Global South, the fast growth of urban centers often results in the creation of informal settlements, characterized by deficiencies in the provision and coverage of basic urban services (e.g., trash collection, sanitation, pest control) and infrastructure (Carvalho-Pereira et al. 2024; Costa et al. 2014; de Oliveira et al. 2024). The resulting environment is highly conductive to rodent infestation, with an abundance of water, food and shelter (Panti-May et al. 2016). Such close coexistence exposes the populations of the settlements to the pathogens carried by rats (Costa, Ribeiro, et al. 2014; Muschetto et al. 2025). The role of rats as a zoonotic pathogen reservoir is arguably one of the most impactful threats posed by our proximity. Rodents host a remarkable diversity of zoonotic pathogens, including viruses, bacteria, unicellular eukary- ote and helminth parasites (Luis et al. 2013; Himsworth et al. 2013; Delaney, Treuting, and Rothenburger 2018). Some of the most historically relevant pathogens have ro- dents as their reservoir, such as Yersinia pestis (Rahelinirina et al. 2021), Leptospira sp. (A. Minter et al. 2017) and Hantavirus (Dearing and Dizney 2010). Depending on the pathogen, rodents can either be direct sources of infection or act as part of the transmission cycle, shedding bacteria to the environment or promoting infective contact with competent hosts that thus infect humans (Himsworth et al. 2013). Important examples of pathogens carried by Norway rats are Leptospira spp. (Feng and Himsworth 2013), Hantavirus (Chen et al. 2023), and Toxoplasma gondii (Bazan et al. 2025). Leptospira spp., the causative agent of leptospirosis, is a genus of bacteria transmitted by water and soil contaminated by the urine of infected hosts such as rats, which are asymptomatic carriers and chronic shedders of the bacteria (Guerra 2009; Tucunduva de Faria et al. 2007). With over one million estimated human cases per year (Costa et al. 2015), the infection can cause asymptomatic/mild forms or evolve into severe and potentially lethal forms such as Weil’s disease and Leptospirosis-associated pulmonary hemor- rhage syndrome (Ko, Goarant, and Picardeau 2009). In Salvador, leptospirosis is a long-standing challenge to public health in impoverished urban communities (Ko et al. 1999; Ribeiro et al. 2008). Hantavirus (Hantaviridae: genus Orthohantavirus) is a genus of negative-sense RNA viruses maintained mainly by small mammals (Bradfute et al. 2024), with several species pathogenic to humans. The clade is divided in Old World Hantaviruses (e.g., Orthohantavirus seoulense [SEOV], Orthohantavirus hantanense [HTNV]), causative agents of Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome, and New World Hantaviruses (e.g., Orthohantavirus andense [ANDV], Orthohantavirus sinnombreense [SNV]), causative agents of Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (Chen et al. 2023). Norway rats are the main reservoirs of Orthohantavirus seoulense, with chronic, nearly asymptomatic infection (Jonsson et al.2010; Meyer and Schmaljohn 2000). SEOV is considered to be cosmopolitan following the worldwide distribution of rats (Himsworth et al. 2013) and has been previously detected in rats in Salvador (Costa et al. 2014). Toxoplasma gondii is an apicomplexan parasite that widely infects warm-blooded animals, causing grave illness in immunocompromised individuals, as well as fetal development issues through congenital…

papers.title_zh: 城市挪威鼠群体中钩端螺旋体与 汉坦病毒 的生态驱动因素差异。

analysis_zh.background: 鼠类控制是关键的公共卫生措施,因为老鼠携带多种人畜共患病原体,且有效的项目必须融合鼠类与病原体生态学。
analysis_zh.methods: 在巴西萨尔瓦多的四个城市贫困社区捕获了120只挪威鼠,并检测了钩端螺旋体;使用环境和人口变量并通过逐步AIC选择,构建了针对钩端螺旋体 (N=109) 和 汉坦病毒 (N=108) 阳性的广义线性模型。
analysis_zh.results: Leptospira阳性率与年龄、Calodium hepaticum瘢痕、伤口、堆积物、开放式下水道渠和未铺砌土壤呈正相关;汉坦病毒阳性率与年龄和堆积物呈正相关,而啮齿动物控制行动和男性性别具有保护作用。
analysis_zh.contribution: 研究表明,钩端螺旋体与 汉坦病毒 的生态驱动因素不同,提示控制措施必须针对特定病原体生态进行定制,以降低人畜共患风险。
analysis_zh.limitations: 在提供的证据中未报告。

papers.title: Hantavirus RNA Detection in Small Mammals and Spatial Association with Human Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome in the West Kazakhstan Region, 2025
papers.abstract: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a zoonotic disease associated with orthohantaviruses maintained in natural rodent hosts. This study assessed the detection and spatial distribution of hantavirus RNA among small mammals in the West Kazakhstan Region in 2025 and compared rodent surveillance findings with human HFRS occurrence. An observational descriptive-analytical study was conducted in August–September 2025 in four districts. A total of 343 small mammals were captured and morphologically identified. Lung tissues were tested using 123 pooled testing units, while 14 specimens were tested individually during the same surveillance campaign. Thus, 137 testing units representing 343 animals were evaluated by real-time and conventional RT-PCR. The minimum infection rate (MIR) was calculated as a descriptive minimum estimate, and a pooled-testing likelihood model was used to account for variation in testing-unit size. Hantavirus RNA was detected in 47/137 testing units, including 45 positive pooled units and two individually positive specimens, corresponding to a descriptive MIR of 13.7%. The model-based individual-level infection probability was estimated at 18.0% (95% profile-likelihood CI: 13.5–23.1%). Positive testing units were observed among Apodemus uralensis, Myodes glareolus, and Microtus arvalis. At the district level, the descriptive MIR ranged from 11.6% in Burlinsky to 19.0% in Chingirlauisky. Sampling sites overlapped spatially with settlements reporting human HFRS cases, including Utvinka, Daryinsk, and Rubezhinskoye; however, spatial coincidence does not establish direct transmission.

analysis.background: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a zoonotic disease linked to orthohantaviruses maintained in rodent hosts (A1).
analysis.methods: An observational descriptive‑analytical study was performed in August–September 2025 across four districts (A3); 343 small mammals were captured and identified (A4); lung tissues from 137 testing units (123 pooled, 14 individual) were examined by real‑time and conventional RT‑PCR (A6).
analysis.results: Hantavirus RNA was found in 47 of 137 testing units, giving a descriptive minimum infection rate of 13.7% (A8); a model‑based individual infection probability was 18.0% (95% CI 13.5–23.1%) (A9); district MIR ranged from 11.6% to 19.0% (A11).
analysis.contribution: The work links rodent hantavirus prevalence with human HFRS case locations, highlighting spatial overlap and informing surveillance priorities (A2, A12).
analysis.limitations: The abstract notes that spatial coincidence does not prove direct transmission and only abstract data are available (A13).

analysis.summary_en: Background: HFRS is a rodent‑borne zoonosis caused by orthohantaviruses (A1). Methods: An observational descriptive‑analytical survey in four districts (Aug‑Sep 2025) captured 343 mammals, whose lung tissues (137 testing units) were tested by RT‑PCR (A3, A4, A6). Results: Hantavirus RNA was detected in 47/137 units (MIR 13.7%); model‑based infection probability 18.0% (95% CI 13.5–23.1%); district MIR 11.6–19.0% (A8, A9, A11). Contribution: Demonstrates spatial overlap between infected rodents and human HFRS cases, supporting targeted surveillance (A2, A12). Limitations: Spatial overlap does not establish transmission and only abstract information is provided (A13).

analysis_zh.background: 肾综合征出血热(HFRS)是一种人畜共患疾病,关联于在啮齿动物宿主中维持的正汉坦病毒es(A1)。
analysis_zh.methods: 2025年8–9月在四个区(A3)开展了一项观察性描述-分析研究;捕获并鉴定了343只小型哺乳动物(A4);对137个检测单元(其中123个为混合样本,14个为单个样本)的肺组织进行实时和常规RT-PCR检测(A6)。
analysis_zh.results: 汉坦病毒 在137个检测单元中检测到RNA阳性47例,描述性最低感染率为13.7%(A8);基于模型的个体感染概率为18.0%(95% CI 13.5–23.1%)(A9);各区的最低感染率(MIR)在11.6%至19.0%之间(A11)。
analysis_zh.contribution: 该研究将啮齿动物汉坦病毒的流行率与人类肾综合征出血热病例分布关联,突出空间重叠并为监测重点提供依据(A2, A12)。
analysis_zh.limitations: 摘要指出,空间重合并不证明直接传播,且仅有摘要数据可用(A13)。

papers.title: Hantaan virus polymerase has an in vitro Terminal Nucleotidyl Transferase activity that is conserved across the Bunyaviricetes class
papers.abstract: Abstract section Bunyaviricetes is a class of segmented negative strand RNA viruses (sNSV) that includes causative agents of severe zoonotic diseases resulting in hemorrhagic fever in humans and livestock. Hantaan virus (HTNV), family Hantaviridae , is an example of life-threatening bunyavirus transmitted by rodents which leads to Hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in humans. Infection relies on the replication and transcription of their tripartite genomes through multifunctional RNA-dependent RNA polymerases (RdRp) in the context of ribonucleoproteins (RNPs) made of one viral RNA fragment, one RdRp and multiple copies of viral nucleoproteins. The RdRp, also known as L protein, performs replication by de novo initiation through a prime-and-realign mechanism while transcription initiates through a cap snatching mechanism, that engages a cap-binding domain and an endonuclease (EN) domain present in the L protein C and N terminal regions, respectively. In this work we show that HTNV L protein has a terminal nucleotidyl transferase (TNTase) activity over double-stranded RNA substrates (dsRNA) in vitro . We show that the TNTase activity is also present in other bunyaviral L proteins by comparing HTNV L protein activity with La Crosse (LACV, family Orthobunyaviridae ) and Crimean Congo Hemorrhagic Fever Virus (CCHFV, family Nairoviridae ) L proteins. Our results show that TNTase activity appears to be a general feature of Bunyaviruses and report the differences on substrate and nucleotide specificity for each family of virus. Importance The L proteins are preferential antiviral targets for the treatment of bunyaviral emerging diseases. Our results provide new ground for the characterization of L protein enzymatic activity in vitro which should be considered for the development activity assays, paramount for the screening of antiviral compounds. Indeed, TNTase activity can be easily misinterpreted as replication activity. We indicate here the key experimental setup and controls that would need to be considered to distinguish both activities. Our in vitro observations pave the way for future investivation of the potential TNTase role(s) in the infected cells. Proposed hypotheses concern potential functions in the preservation of genome integrity, the prevention of RIG-I innate immune response activation, or modification of RNA metabolism in the cell cytoplasm. The TNTase activity assays we describe here finally provide a straightforward biochemical approach for screening of inhibitors targeting RdRp activity.

Our results show that TNTase activity appears to be a general feature of Bunyaviruses and report the differences on substrate and nucleotide specificity for each family of virus. Importance The L proteins are preferential antiviral targets for the treatment of bunyaviral emerging diseases. Our results provide new ground for the characterization of L protein enzymatic activity in vitro which should be considered for the development activity assays, paramount for the screening of antiviral compounds. Indeed, TNTase activity can be easily misinterpreted as replication activity. We indicate here the key experimental setup and controls that would need to be considered to distinguish both activities. Our in vitro observations pave the way for future investivation of the potential TNTase role(s) in the infected cells. Proposed hypotheses concern potential functions in the preservation of genome integrity, the prevention of RIG-I innate immune response activation, or modification of RNA metabolism in the cell cytoplasm. The TNTase activity assays we describe here finally provide a straightforward biochemical approach for screening of inhibitors targeting RdRp activity.

papers.title: Multi-omics Reveals Divergent Endothelial Molecular Responses to New and Old World Hantaviruses.
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses cause vascular leakage syndromes that vary in clinical manifestation and severity. Although tissue tropism contributes to these differences, both Old and New World hantaviruses infect endothelial cells, where species-specific disease phenotypes remain poorly understood. Here we integrated time-resolved global RNA sequencing, mass spectrometry proteomics, and phosphoproteomics of human endothelial cells infected with New World Andes virus (ANDV) or Old World Hantaan virus (HTNV). Despite equivalent early viral RNA and protein levels, ANDV elicited a stronger innate immune protein response, preceding its restriction while HTNV replication continued. At later stages of infection, HTNV induced downregulation of cytoskeletal and junctional protein phosphorylation, accompanied by visual disruption of cellular actin architecture. Additionally, ANDV induced heightened activity of ERBB-family kinases, whose chemical inhibition by neratinib and afatinib reduced viral replication. Together, these data define species-specific responses in endothelial cells, identify druggable host targets, and reveal mechanisms with relevance to divergent vascular leakage symptomology.

papers.title: Habitat-Mediated Spillover Risk of Andes Hantavirus in Oligoryzomys longicaudatus: A Mechanistic Eco-Epidemiological Model.
papers.abstract: Andes hantavirus (ANDV) is a rodent-borne orthohantavirus associated with hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome in southern South America. Its maintenance and spillover risk depend on the ecology of its principal reservoir, Oligoryzomys longicaudatus, and on environmental changes that alter habitat availability, host abundance, and human-rodent interfaces. We developed a mechanistic eco-epidemiological model that couples effective habitat cover to an SIR framework for ANDV transmission in O. longicaudatus. Habitat degradation and compensatory restoration modify rodent carrying capacity, natality, and the force of infection, which depends on infected host load relative to instantaneous ecological capacity. We derived the habitat equilibrium, the basic reproduction number R0, and the time-dependent effective reproduction number Re(t) and evaluated infection-burden and threshold indicators across degradation-restoration scenarios. The analysis shows that R0 is independent of equilibrium habitat cover because susceptible abundance scales with carrying capacity at the disease-free equilibrium. In contrast, Re(t), cumulative incidence, and infected load depend on transient habitat-mediated crowding. Restoration increases reservoir abundance and absolute infection burden, whereas degradation can reduce abundance while increasing crowding-driven transmission pressure and prolonging supercritical windows. These results identify ecological conditions under which habitat change may intensify reservoir infection pressure and guide One Health surveillance at human-rodent interfaces.

papers.title_zh: 安第斯病毒 [PDI0109] (ANDV) 在长尾鼠 Oligoryzomys longicaudatus 中的栖息地介导跨种传播风险:一种机制生态流行病学模型。

analysis_zh.background: 安第斯病毒 汉坦病毒 (ANDV) 是一种啮齿动物传播的病毒,导致南美洲南部的肾综合征出血热,其跨种传播风险取决于主要储存宿主 Oligoryzomys longicaudatus 的生态以及影响宿主丰度和人‐啮齿动物界面的栖息地变化。
analysis_zh.methods: 作者构建了一个机制生态流行病学模型,将有效栖息地覆盖率与 O. longicaudatus 中 ANDV 传播的 SIR 框架耦合,推导出栖息地平衡、基本再生数 R0 以及在退化‐恢复情景下随时间变化的有效再生数 Re(t)。
analysis_zh.results: 分析表明,R0 与栖息地平衡覆盖率无关,因为易感个体丰度随容纳量成比例;相反,Re(t)、累计发病率和感染负荷取决于瞬时的栖息地导致的拥挤程度。恢复会增加储存宿主丰度和绝对感染负担,而退化则可能降低丰度,却提升因拥挤驱动的传播压力并延长超临界窗口。
analysis_zh.contribution: 这些结果明确了栖息地变化可能加剧宿主感染压力的生态条件,并为人畜接口的 One Health 监测提供指导。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅提供摘要;未报告详细数据、参数化和验证。

papers.title: AI-generated medical realism and hantavirus misinformation: a new public health threat?
papers.abstract: The widespread availability of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has substantially reshaped the health-information environment compared with the COVID-19 pandemic. Contemporary AI tools can rapidly generate highly realistic medical-looking content from text, including laboratory reports, radiological images, histological slides, and institutional clinical documentation. During infectious disease outbreaks, such simulated medical content may exploit the visual authority traditionally associated with healthcare institutions and influence public risk perception. During media coverage of the May 2026 Andes virus (ANDV) alert in Italy, news outlets published realistic AI-generated medical imagery depicting hantavirus diagnostic reports, hospital-associated laboratory materials, and outbreak-response scenes linked to real healthcare institutions. One image, in particular, reproduced the visual identity of a real laboratory report produced at "Luigi Sacco" University Hospital despite displaying multiple inconsistencies. In some additional examples, AI generation was not clearly disclosed despite the use of recognizable institutional names and logos. This phenomenon has the potential to extend beyond isolated misinformation events. Emerging evidence indicates that experts may struggle to reliably distinguish AI-generated biomedical and radiological images from authentic materials, raising concern that future infectious disease outbreaks may occur within an information ecosystem increasingly shaped by visually persuasive synthetic media. Such content may amplify public anxiety, distort perceptions of authority, and erode trust in institutions. Synthetic medical realism should therefore be considered a potential emerging category of public-health risk during infectious disease emergencies that requires coordinated action from institutions and regulators developing verification systems, while news media, platforms, and publishers implement AI-disclosure standards and guidelines for synthetic biomedical content.

papers.title: Generation and Characterization of the Human Anti-HTNV Antibody KJJ4.
papers.abstract: Hantaan virus (HTNV) is the predominant causative agent of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in China, yet no specific antiviral therapy is currently available. Neutralizing antibodies (NAbs) represent a promising strategy, but most existing anti-HTNV NAbs are heterologous and carry immunogenicity risks. Here, two fully human antibodies from a previously established human anti-HTNV phage display library were generated and characterized. KJJ3, a VL-VL tandem antibody derived from clone 3-12, showed weak binding to inactivated HTNV and minimal neutralizing activity (IC50 = 27.12 μg/mL). However, KJJ4, an engineered IgG4 antibody derived from clone 4-19 and carrying the S108P hinge mutation to prevent Fab-arm exchange, bound inactivated HTNV antigen and recombinant glycoprotein Gn (residues 19-371) in a dose-dependent manner, with only weak binding to Gc. Surface plasmon resonance yielded an association rate constant of 4.70 × 103 M-1s-1, a dissociation rate constant of 3.06 × 10-3 s-1, and an equilibrium dissociation constant of 650 nM for monomeric Gn19-371. In a Vero E6 focus-reduction microneutralization assay, KJJ4 neutralized HTNV in vitro with an IC50 of 2.879 μg/mL. These data establish KJJ4 as a fully human anti-HTNV antibody with experimentally defined in vitro binding and neutralizing activity, warranting further evaluation in animal models of HTNV infection.

analysis.background: Hantaan virus (HTNV) is the main cause of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in China and lacks a specific antiviral therapy.
analysis.methods: Two fully human antibodies were derived from a human anti‑HTNV phage‑display library, engineered (IgG4 with S108P hinge), and evaluated by dose‑dependent ELISA, surface plasmon resonance (SPR) for kinetic constants, and a Vero E6 focus‑reduction microneutralization assay.
analysis.results: KJJ4 bound inactivated HTNV and recombinant Gn (residues 19‑371) with an SPR K_D of 650 nM (k_a = 4.70 × 10^3 M⁻¹s⁻¹, k_d = 3.06 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹) and neutralized HTNV in vitro with an IC₅₀ of 2.879 μg/mL, whereas the related KJJ3 showed weak binding and minimal neutralization (IC₅₀ = 27.12 μg/mL).
analysis.contribution: The study provides the first fully human anti‑HTNV IgG4 antibody with defined in‑vitro binding and neutralizing activity, supporting its further testing in animal models for therapeutic development.
analysis.limitations: Findings are limited to in‑vitro assays reported in the abstract; no animal‑model or clinical data are presented.

analysis.summary_en: Background: HTNV causes HFRS in China and has no specific antiviral. Methods: Human antibodies from a phage‑display library were engineered (IgG4 S108P) and assessed by ELISA, SPR, and Vero E6 microneutralization. Results: KJJ4 bound HTNV Gn (K_D = 650 nM) and neutralized virus (IC₅₀ = 2.879 μg/mL); KJJ3 showed weak activity. Contribution: Introduces a fully human anti‑HTNV antibody for further pre‑clinical evaluation. Limitations: Data are limited to in‑vitro assays in the abstract, with no in‑vivo validation.

papers.title: Integrated Analysis of Human Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome Cases and Rodent Hantavirus Surveillance in Zhejiang Province, China, 2025.
papers.abstract: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), caused by Seoul orthohantavirus (SEOV) and Hantaan orthohantavirus (HTNV), remains a neglected rodent-borne zoonosis with persistent residual spillover risk in low-incidence regions of China. This study assessed human HFRS occurrence and small-mammal hantavirus surveillance signals in small-mammal hosts across Zhejiang Province, China, in 2025. Reported human cases were obtained from the National Notifiable Disease Surveillance System, and animal host surveillance was conducted at five designated monitoring sites. A total of 107 HFRS cases were reported, occurring year-round with peaks in June and December and showing spatial heterogeneity, presenting a predominance of males, adults aged ≥40 years, and farmers. Animal host surveillance captured 617 small mammals (566 rodents and 51 shrews) from 15,457 valid trap-nights, with Apodemus agrarius (30.31%) and Rattus norvegicus (29.98%) as the dominant species. Sixteen animals were positive for hantavirus RNA and/or antibody, including 12 for hantavirus RNA and 6 antibody-positive animals; two were positive for both markers. Positive animals were detected in multiple species, including Niviventer confucianus, R. norvegicus, Rattus losea, A. agrarius, Suncus murinus, and Rattus tanezumi. Human incidence, small-mammal density, host species composition, and hantavirus-positive rates were not fully concordant across surveillance sites. Our findings reveal sustained cryptic orthohantavirus circulation in low-endemic Zhejiang, highlighting that integrated human-reservoir One Health surveillance is indispensable for precise spillover risk prediction and targeted zoonotic disease intervention.

analysis.methods: The study assessed human HFRS occurrence and small‑mammal hantavirus surveillance across Zhejiang Province in 2025 (A2); human cases were obtained from the National Notifiable Disease Surveillance System and animal surveillance was performed at five designated sites (A3).
analysis.results: A total of 107 HFRS cases were reported year‑round with peaks in June and December, mainly affecting males, adults ≥40 years, and farmers (A4); 617 small mammals (566 rodents, 51 shrews) were trapped over 15,457 trap‑nights, dominated by Apodemus agrarius (30.31%) and Rattus norvegicus (29.98%) (A5); sixteen animals were hantavirus RNA‑ and/or antibody‑positive, including 12 RNA‑positive and 6 antibody‑positive, with two animals positive for both markers and detections across multiple species (A6‑A10); human incidence, small‑mammal density, host composition, and hantavirus‑positive rates were not fully concordant across sites (A11).

analysis.limitations: Only the abstract is provided, limiting detail on study design, statistical analyses, and broader context (abstract_only).

analysis.summary_en: Background: HFRS caused by SEOV and HTNV is a neglected rodent‑borne zoonosis with persistent spillover risk in low‑incidence China (A1). Methods: Human cases from the national surveillance system and small‑mammal surveillance at five sites in Zhejiang were analyzed for 2025 (A2‑A3). Results: 107 HFRS cases occurred year‑round, mainly males ≥40 years and farmers; 617 mammals were trapped, with 16 hantavirus‑positive animals across several species; human incidence and animal infection patterns were not fully aligned across sites (A4‑A11). Contribution: The study shows cryptic orthohantavirus circulation and highlights the need for integrated One Health surveillance (A12). Limitations: Only abstract data are available, restricting detail on methods and analyses (abstract_only).

papers.title_zh: 2025年中国浙江省人类肾综合征出血热病例与啮齿动物汉坦病毒监测的综合分析

analysis_zh.background: 肾综合征出血热(HFRS),由首尔病毒(SEOV)和汉滩病毒(HTNV)引起,是一种被忽视的啮齿动物媒介人畜共患病,在中国低发地区仍存在持续的溢出风险 (A1)。
analysis_zh.methods: 本研究评估了2025年浙江省的人类HFRS发生情况及小型哺乳动物汉坦病毒监测 (A2);人类病例来源于国家法定传染病监测系统,动物监测在五个指定地点进行 (A3)。
analysis_zh.results: 全年共报告107例HFRS病例,峰值出现在6月和12月,主要影响男性、≥40岁的成人以及农民 (A4);在15,457个捕鼠夜中捕获617只小型哺乳动物(566只啮齿动物,51只鼩鼱),以田野鼠 (Apodemus agrarius) (30.31%) 和挪威鼠 (Rattus norvegicus) (29.98%) 为主 (A5);16只动物检测出汉坦病毒 RNA和/或抗体阳性,其中12例RNA阳性,6例抗体阳性,两只动物两种标记均阳性,且在多种物种中均有检测 (A6‐A10);人类发病率、小型哺乳动物密度、宿主组成以及汉坦病毒阳性率在各地点并不完全一致 (A11)。
analysis_zh.contribution: 研究结果显示,低流行的浙江地区仍存在持续的隐匿正汉坦病毒循环,并强调综合的人类‐储备One Health监测对于精准预测溢出风险和实施有针对性的干预至关重要 (A12)。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅提供摘要,限制了对研究设计、统计分析及更广背景的细节描述 (abstract_only)。
